@@138608655 <h> Palestinians in Lebanon : A Lifetime of Exile Without Equal Rights <p> For more than seventy-five years , Palestinian refugees in Lebanon have lived in one of the world 's longest and most complex refugee crises . What began as a temporary displacement following the 1948 Arab-Israeli war has evolved into a multigenerational reality in which hundreds of thousands of Palestinians remain trapped between a homeland they can not return to and a host country that has never fully embraced them as equal members of society . <p> Unlike most refugee populations , Palestinians in Lebanon occupy a unique legal and political position . They are denied Lebanese citizenship and continue to face restrictions affecting employment , property ownership , social protection , and economic participation . Although Lebanese authorities have long argued that these measures are necessary to preserve the Palestinians ' right of return and prevent permanent resettlement , critics contend that the result has been decades of institutional discrimination that has left entire generations marginalized . <p> Economic exclusion remains one of the defining characteristics of Palestinian life in Lebanon . Despite gradual legal reforms over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accessing stable and well-paid employment . Many are forced into informal labor markets where wages are low , contracts are absent , and legal protections are virtually nonexistent . Young university graduates frequently discover that education alone can not overcome structural discrimination , leaving many with limited prospects for financial independence . <p> The consequences extend far beyond employment . Poverty rates inside many refugee camps remain significantly higher than national averages , while deteriorating living conditions have become increasingly visible . Narrow alleyways , overcrowded housing , unreliable electricity , inadequate sanitation , and aging infrastructure characterize many camps established decades ago as temporary shelters but which have since become permanent communities . Lebanon 's ongoing economic collapse has only deepened these hardships , pushing vulnerable refugee families further into poverty . <p> For many Palestinians , the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East ( UNRWA ) represents the primary source of education , healthcare , and humanitarian assistance . However , repeated funding crises have weakened the agency 's capacity to deliver essential services , increasing uncertainty for refugees who already @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ global conflicts , many Palestinians fear that their humanitarian needs are gradually disappearing from the international agenda . <p> Security inside certain refugee camps presents another layer of complexity . Historical political arrangements have resulted in limited state authority within parts of some camps , allowing multiple Palestinian factions and armed groups to maintain varying degrees of influence . Human rights observers , journalists , and researchers have documented allegations that some residents have experienced intimidation , coercion , or exploitation by particular armed actors seeking political , financial , or social control . Such allegations deserve careful investigation and accountability . <p> Nevertheless , it is essential to distinguish between the actions of specific individuals or factions and the broader Palestinian refugee community . Many Palestinians themselves are among the strongest advocates for the rule of law , peaceful governance , and community reform inside the camps . Civil society organizations , youth initiatives , educators , and local leaders continue working under difficult circumstances to reduce violence , expand educational opportunities , and strengthen social cohesion . <p> Palestinian refugees also face social discrimination beyond the camps . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ times , portrayed Palestinians as contributors to Lebanon 's political instability or economic difficulties . Such narratives often ignore the reality that Palestinian refugees possess limited political power and remain among the country 's most economically vulnerable populations . Generalized accusations risk reinforcing prejudice while diverting attention from the structural causes of Lebanon 's broader crises . <p> International human rights organizations have repeatedly emphasized that access to basic human rights should not be conditional upon nationality or refugee status . The right to work , adequate housing , healthcare , education , and legal protection are recognized under international human rights standards . Expanding these rights does not necessarily imply permanent naturalization , nor does it negate the internationally recognized right of Palestinian refugees to seek a just and durable solution consistent with international law . <p> The international community also bears responsibility . Decades of diplomatic stagnation regarding the Palestinian question have left refugee populations in neighboring countries living in prolonged uncertainty . Humanitarian assistance alone can not substitute for durable political solutions , nor can financial aid replace meaningful legal protections . <p> Ultimately , the story @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It is about generations born into legal uncertainty , economic exclusion , and political limbo despite having committed no crime other than being born refugees . Their lives demonstrate the human cost of unresolved conflicts that continue to shape the Middle East decades after the original displacement occurred . <p> A society 's commitment to human rights is measured not by how it treats the powerful , but by how it treats those with the fewest protections . Ensuring dignity , equal legal safeguards , and access to fundamental rights for Palestinian refugees should not be viewed as a political concession . It should be recognized as a moral and humanitarian obligation consistent with the universal principles of justice and human rights . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Husein Mahmoud Saleh is an independent writer and political analyst specializing in Middle Eastern affairs , with a particular focus on human rights , conflict , forced displacement , and regional politics . Yet its true weight can not be measured in pages . It is measured instead in half-recorded names , in ages repeated with painful regularity , and in the relentless arithmetic of a war in which children have become the primary victims . <p> Some reports inform . This one indicts . What is the report 's essential argument ? <p> Central Claim <p> The killing of Palestinian children in Gaza was not accidental . Nor was it merely the tragic by-product of urban warfare . It was a pattern . And that pattern , the Commission argues , is evidence of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ children were targeted precisely because they are children . Their deaths , injuries , and disabilities strike at the biological and emotional continuity of the Palestinian people as a group . <p> This is where the report moves beyond documenting individual horrors to advancing the gravest charge in international law : genocide . According to the Commission , the deliberate killing of children is " a key element " in establishing genocidal intent . <p> How the Evidence Was Built ? <p> How did the Commission arrive at this conclusion ? <p> Its methodology , explained early in the report , is painstaking by design . Israel denied the Commission access to the Occupied Palestinian Territory and declined every request for information . Faced with those obstacles , the Commission drew on multiple sources of evidence . <p> It collected and verified thousands of open-source items . It conducted both remote and in-person interviews with victims and witnesses , including children , always with the informed consent of a parent or guardian . It engaged two independent forensic pathologists to examine CT scans , X-rays , photographs , and videos @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Commission relied instead on material already gathered by other organisations . <p> It also used geolocation , chrono-location ( digital forensic technique used to determine the date and time of an image , video , or recorded event ) , and metadata analysis to verify images and footage . In other words , it relied on the same forensic techniques used in modern war crimes investigations and prosecutions . <p> It is a methodology built to withstand the very allegation of bias that Israel has repeatedly levelled against it . <p> The Numbers <p> The numbers alone are enough to stop the breath . Between 7 October 2023 and 7 October 2025 , the inqury finds that at least 20,179 children were killed and 44,143 injured in Gaza , " constituting 30 percent of those killed and 26 percent of those injured during this period , " a proportion higher than in any earlier round of hostilities , when children accounted for roughly 24 percent of fatalities . <p> At least 5,031 children under the age of five died , including 1,029 infants under one year old and some @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the rubble , according to figures from Save the Children cited by the evidence . <p> In the West Bank , 213 children were killed , 206 of them boys . The investigation reads this pattern as evidence of the deliberate , gendered targeting of Palestinian boyhood itself . <p> The Destruction of Childhood 's Institutions <p> The destruction extended far beyond lives . According to UN assessments cited by the Commission , Gaza 's educational system was systematically dismantled . More than 95 percent of schools , over 530 school buildings , had been damaged or destroyed by late 2025 . All of Gaza 's universities and higher-education institutions were affected , with most campuses rendered unusable . What was lost was not only infrastructure , but the ordinary architecture of childhood itself : classrooms , playgrounds , libraries , exams , friendships , and the expectation that a future could be planned . The report argues that the assault on education was not merely collateral damage . It was part of the destruction of the conditions necessary for Palestinian society to sustain and reproduce itself . <p> It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of one or both parents , what UNICEF has described as the largest orphan crisis in modern history , and more than 3,000 children lost both parents entirely . <p> Beyond Statistics <p> The real power of Muralidhar 's report lies beyond the statistics . @@138608676 <h> Why Muslim-Majority States Failed to Stop the Wars in Gaza , Lebanon , and Sudan ? <p> The devastating conflicts in Gaza , Lebanon , and Sudan have exposed significant limitations in the collective diplomatic and strategic influence of Muslim-majority states . Despite repeated emergency summits , strong public condemnations , humanitarian assistance , and widespread public solidarity across the Islamic world , these conflicts have continued with catastrophic humanitarian consequences . According to the United Nations , the war in Gaza has resulted in tens of thousands of deaths and injuries , widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure , and the displacement of most of the territory 's population . In Sudan , the civil war that erupted in April 2023 has displaced well over 14 million people and created what the UN describes as one of the world 's largest humanitarian crises . In Lebanon , recurrent hostilities along the Israel-Lebanon border have displaced hundreds of thousands of civilians and severely damaged infrastructure . The inability of Muslim-majority governments to halt these conflicts reflects not a lack of concern but a combination of geopolitical fragmentation , institutional weakness @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ international system . <p> One of the foremost reasons for the limited influence of Muslim-majority states is the absence of political unity . The Islamic world consists of 57 member states of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation ( OIC ) , representing nearly two billion Muslims -- approximately one-quarter of the global population . Together , these countries account for roughly 8 -- 9 per cent of global GDP despite possessing nearly 70 per cent of the world 's proven oil reserves and around 40 per cent of natural gas reserves . This apparent contradiction illustrates that while many Muslim-majority countries possess substantial natural resources , they do not function as a coherent geopolitical bloc . Instead , regional rivalries , differing security priorities , ideological differences , and national interests often prevent coordinated action . Competing foreign policy objectives among Middle Eastern , African , and Asian member states have frequently undermined efforts to formulate unified responses to regional crises . <p> The wars in Gaza and Lebanon particularly demonstrated these divisions . Some governments demanded immediate ceasefires , imposed diplomatic protests , or expanded humanitarian assistance , while @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ concerns , or economic interests . Several countries have normalised or maintained diplomatic relations with Israel , while others have no diplomatic engagement . These differing approaches limited the possibility of presenting a united diplomatic front capable of exerting significant international pressure . Similarly , in Sudan , neighbouring Muslim-majority states pursued separate mediation initiatives , often reflecting their security and regional interests rather than a single coordinated peace process . <p> Institutional limitations further explain the inability to influence these conflicts decisively . Although the OIC is the second-largest intergovernmental organisation after the United Nations , its institutional powers remain largely consultative . Unlike military alliances or regional organisations with enforcement mechanisms , the OIC can not impose binding sanctions , authorise collective military operations , or enforce compliance with its resolutions . Its decisions depend entirely on voluntary implementation by member states . Consequently , extraordinary summits and ministerial declarations have primarily produced political statements and humanitarian commitments rather than enforceable collective action . <p> Economic and military dependence on major global powers also constrains the foreign policy options of many Muslim-majority governments . Several states maintain extensive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Russia , or China , relying on imported military equipment , intelligence cooperation , financial investment , technology transfers , and security guarantees . According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute , a significant proportion of arms imported by Middle Eastern states originate from the United States and Europe . Such strategic relationships inevitably influence diplomatic calculations during regional conflicts . Governments must balance domestic public opinion with broader national security interests , economic development objectives , and long-term strategic partnerships . <p> Another important limitation lies in the absence of a collective defence or crisis-response mechanism comparable to alliances like the North Atlantic Treaty Organization . While countries such as Saudi Arabia , T ? rkiye , Pakistan , Egypt , Indonesia , and others possess substantial military capabilities individually , these forces do not operate under a unified command capable of coordinated regional intervention . Furthermore , military intervention in conflicts such as Gaza or Lebanon would involve profound legal , political , and strategic risks , including the possibility of wider regional escalation . Consequently , most governments have preferred diplomatic engagement , humanitarian assistance , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The structure of the international system also limits the capacity of Muslim-majority states to shape outcomes . The United Nations Security Council remains the principal body responsible for maintaining international peace and security . However , no Muslim-majority country possesses permanent membership or veto power . Consequently , resolutions relating to Gaza or other regional conflicts often become subject to broader geopolitical competition among permanent members rather than reflecting the collective preferences of developing countries . This structural imbalance reduces the effectiveness of diplomatic initiatives originating from Muslim-majority states alone . <p> Domestic political and economic challenges further reduce the capacity of governments to sustain prolonged international engagement . Many Muslim-majority countries continue to address high youth unemployment , inflation , governance reforms , terrorism , refugee management , debt burdens , and climate-related vulnerabilities . The World Bank has repeatedly highlighted the economic pressures affecting several Middle Eastern and African economies recently . Governments facing significant domestic challenges often have limited financial and political resources available for sustained diplomatic initiatives abroad . <p> Sudan presents a particularly revealing example of these limitations . Unlike Gaza and Lebanon , where @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ primarily involves domestic political and military actors . Since fighting began in April 2023 , well over 14 million people have been displaced , while nearly 25 million people require humanitarian assistance , according to United Nations estimates . Despite efforts by regional groups and nearby countries to help , different outside interests , a lack of trust between Sudanese groups , and weak enforcement has stopped lasting peace talks . The Sudan case demonstrates that religious affinity alone can not overcome complex political , ethnic , economic , and military dynamics . <p> Humanitarian assistance has remained one of the most visible contributions made by Muslim-majority governments . Countries including Saudi Arabia , Qatar , T ? rkiye , the United Arab Emirates , Kuwait , Malaysia , Indonesia , and others have provided substantial financial assistance , medical supplies , food aid , and refugee support to populations affected by these conflicts . Numerous charitable organisations have also mobilised significant resources for emergency relief efforts . While these efforts have undoubtedly alleviated human suffering , humanitarian assistance can not substitute for political settlements or conflict resolution . Without @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , relief efforts primarily address humanitarian consequences rather than the underlying causes of war . <p> Another important factor is the increasing diversity of strategic priorities across the Muslim world . The security concerns of Southeast Asian countries differ significantly from those of North African , Gulf , Central Asian , or Sub-Saharan African states . Some governments prioritise maritime security , while others prioritise economic diversification , counterterrorism , border disputes , energy security , or technological development . These varying priorities make it difficult to establish a unified foreign policy agenda capable of sustained collective action during international crises . <p> Public opinion throughout many Muslim-majority societies has generally expressed strong solidarity with civilians affected by conflicts in Gaza , Lebanon , and Sudan . Large demonstrations , charitable campaigns , parliamentary debates , and public statements have reflected widespread humanitarian concern . However , foreign policy decisions ultimately remain the responsibility of sovereign governments , which must simultaneously consider international law , regional stability , economic interests , diplomatic commitments , and national security . Consequently , government policies may not always fully reflect popular expectations regarding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Muslim-majority states to stop the wars in Gaza , Lebanon , and Sudan reflects a complex interaction of geopolitical fragmentation , institutional weakness , competing national interests , international power dynamics , economic constraints , and domestic priorities rather than a lack of humanitarian concern . Although these countries collectively represent nearly one-quarter of humanity and possess considerable economic and strategic resources , their influence remains constrained by the absence of unified political action and effective regional institutions . Palestine Action , described by their founders as " a direct-action protest group aimed at preventing military targets in the UK from facilitating gross abuses of international law " , had made its stock and trade targeting Israeli arms manufacturers such as Elbit Systems and businesses with links to the Israeli arms trade . The proscription followed the group 's break-in at RAF Brize Norton , where two aircraft were spray painted . In the proscribed list , which includes such violent luminaries as Boko Haram and Islamic State , Palestine Action is hysterically assessed as an entity that " prepares for terrorism " and " promotes and encourages terrorism . These involved five factors intended to constrain the office holder 's discretion . The resort to " other factors " would have to be read with that constraining purpose in mind . <p> The Court also found that a fair balance between the rights of individuals to free speech ( Article 10 of the European Convention of Human Rights ) and freedom of assembly under Article 11 of the ECHR as against the national security and protection of the rights of others ( Articles 10.2 and 11.2 of the ECHR ) had not been struck . Article 17 of the Convention -- the prohibition of an abuse of rights -- was what counted in her mind . <p> The Court of Appeal went so far as to admit that the rights of those holding placards opposing genocide and supporting the Palestinian cause " may be affected by proscription , because they may be dissuaded by it from exercising their lawful individual rights to free speech and freedom of assembly . @@138608693 <h> Palestine And The Illusion of Historical Determinism <p> A quarter of a century ago , I criticized August Comte 's theory of the three stages , which sought to establish universal laws of history . That idea later influenced Marxism in the form of what became known as historical determinism . My view then and it remains my view today is that history , unlike the natural sciences , does not operate according to rigid universal laws . Rather , it is shaped by a complex web of interacting political , social , economic , cultural , and human factors , making any attempt to reduce it to a linear path or to fixed historical laws fundamentally misleading . Many major ideologies have relied on such assumptions to justify their policies . Today , for example , we repeatedly hear rhetoric about a " New Middle East , " often presented as though it were the inevitable outcome of history , when in reality it reflects political projects , including imperial and Zionist ambitions to reshape and dominate the region . Moral progress is the goal but never guaranteed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to this position . He argued that history is influenced by factors that can not be predicted in advance . If I were asked today whether I had anticipated the unprecedented global wave of solidarity that followed the events of October 7 , my answer would be no . Yet the course of events produced a worldwide movement that may , in its breadth and reach , have surpassed the international mobilization witnessed during the Vietnam War . <p> I expressed similar reservations in an article published in Al Sharq Al Awsat in 1994 , when I discussed Francis Fukuyama 's famous thesis , The End of History . My argument then remains my argument today : his conclusion that liberal democracy represented the final stage of humanity 's political evolution lacked objectivity because history is never closed . It remains open to unforeseen possibilities , unexpected reversals , and new beginnings . <p> For me , the " end of history " can only mean the end of a particular historical phase not the end of history itself . Every historical era eventually gives way to another , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for better or for worse . <p> It is in this sense that I view the current decline of the Zionist narrative . In my assessment , the events in Gaza have marked the beginning of a new historical phase by revealing that several of the pillars that sustained the Zionist project for decades have begun to weaken . Israel undoubtedly retains overwhelming military power . Yet military superiority alone is no longer sufficient to sustain political and moral legitimacy or to preserve a dominant narrative . I believe that the broader foundations of support for the Zionist project have been significantly eroded for several reasons : <p> The extraordinary resilience shown in Gaza . <p> The war in Gaza and the widespread accusations that Israel has committed serious violations of international law , which , in the eyes of many around the world , have exposed realities that had long been obscured . <p> The transformative role of social media in documenting events and bypassing traditional gatekeepers of information . <p> The unprecedented global wave of solidarity , driven above all by a younger generation with access to diverse @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ argue that the " end of history " in this context signifies the end of an era in which the Zionist narrative enjoyed broad dominance across much of the West . A new global memory is emerging one shaped less by official narratives than by direct access to events through digital media and multiple sources of information . How this transformation ultimately unfolds will depend on future political developments , which may either accelerate or slow the process . Yet I believe that the period of unquestioned dominance once enjoyed by that narrative has ended , and that restoring it to its former position will be exceedingly difficult . <p> Although the new always emerges from the old , history remains an open book . Human societies are capable of surprising transformations that defy deterministic predictions . Even the religious belief that good will ultimately triumph over evil should not be mistaken for a historical law . It expresses a moral aspiration rather than an empirical certainty . Justice , freedom , and equality are not inevitable outcomes of history ; they are achievements won through struggle , perseverance , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Its future is shaped by the choices that people make and by the conflicts through which those choices are contested . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Salim Nazzal is a Palestinian Norwegian researcher , lecturer playwright and poet , wrote more than 26 books such as Perspectives on thought , culture and political sociology , in thought , culture and ideology , the road to Baghdad <p> Palestinian Territory -- The Guardian 's recent report on a draft resolution granting legal immunity to the Board of Peace , its members , staff , contractors , and associated forces for actions in the Gaza Strip is ... <h> Support Countercurrents <p> Countercurrents.org is on annual fundraising drive . @@138639269 <h> Nutty Communists of Naples in Italy <p> Naples is the largest city in southern Italy and the third largest in the country . Although the city is widely known as the home of pizza , its culinary diversity and local seafood delicacies can rival any global metropolis . However , the overwhelming focus on pizza often overshadows its other local treasures . From art and music scenes to concerts and theatre festivals -- and , of course , pizza festivals -- there is something for everyone to enjoy every day . It represents a rare fusion of Greek and Roman civilisations . Over the centuries , Naples has witnessed the rise and fall of empires , emperors , kings , kingdoms , occupations , and wars -- making it a city steeped in history and culture . <p> During the Second World War , Naples also experienced the early heydays of American imperialism , which created a thriving market for the sex trade in the city . @@138668830 <h> On the Roots of the Arab Decline <p> There is no doubt that the establishment of Israel and the ensuing Arab-Israeli conflict played a significant role in strengthening revolutionary and radical ideologies in the Arab world . Until the 1940s , Enlightenment thought remained influential and , in many cases , addressed the fundamental problems facing Arab societies . The Lebanese thinker Shibli Shumayyil observed that Europe 's modernization began with religious reform , which later paved the way for political reform . Taha Hussein championed the idea of education as a universal right , Ahmad Lutfi al-Sayyid emphasized constitutionalism and individual rights , and Qasim Amin advocated women 's education and emancipation . <p> This intellectual trajectory changed dramatically after the 1948 Arab-Israeli War , which ended with the Palestinian Nakba and the defeat of the Arab armies . The conflict ushered in an era in which politics and culture became increasingly militarized . The ideals of the Arab Renaissance gradually receded amid an atmosphere of continuous confrontation , while successive wars with Israel supported by Western powers deepened feelings of frustration and defeat across much of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ had enjoyed considerable prestige among Arab intellectuals , who regarded Europe as a model of democracy , constitutional government , and human rights . Over time , however , this perception weakened as many Arabs came to believe that Western governments consistently supported Israel politically and militarily . As a result , distrust of the West -- and , in many cases , hostility toward its policies became increasingly widespread . <p> This climate profoundly influenced a new generation . Gamal Abdel Nasser himself wrote of a generation shaped by defeat and conflict . For many , restoring dignity appeared possible only through confrontation rather than gradual reform . Revolutionary ideologies of various kinds therefore gained appeal , while confidence in peaceful , incremental political change steadily declined . <p> The experience of George Habash illustrates this transformation . In his memoirs , he recounts the entry of Jewish forces into his hometown of Lydda during the 1948 war and describes killings , expulsions , and humiliation . He concluded that the coming era would be one of revenge and resistance . Significantly , the first organization he led was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and emotional mood of that period . <p> Against this backdrop , several Arab monarchies that had witnessed the early flowering of Enlightenment ideas were overthrown . Military officers came to power under the banners of liberation , revenge , and radical change . Their rise encouraged the spread of secular revolutionary ideologies , particularly Arab nationalism and socialism , which were embodied in many of the political movements of the 1950s and 1960s . <p> The atmosphere of permanent conflict also hindered the peaceful development of Arab societies . This can be seen in the weakness of civil society institutions , the fragility of constitutional politics , and the limited development of a political culture based on the peaceful transfer of power . <p> Within this context emerged the notion of the " benevolent despot " the idea that a strong ruler might lead the nation toward progress even at the expense of political freedom . This concept has often been associated , in one form or another , with the reformist tradition represented by Muhammad Abduh . For many Arabs , Gamal Abdel Nasser came to embody the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ achieving modernization . The ideal of the heroic redeemer , moreover , has deep roots in Arab historical memory , where figures such as Saladin continue to symbolize unity and deliverance . <p> In my view , these developments contributed to weakening rational and liberal currents within Arab societies while allowing more traditional patterns of thought to endure . Although the revolutionary regimes introduced important reforms in education , industry , and infrastructure , modernization often remained institutional rather than cultural . Traditional social attitudes persisted , particularly in rural areas where the majority of the population lived . This , in turn , created fertile ground for the later resurgence of Islamist movements as Arab nationalism and socialism gradually declined . <p> Nevertheless , it would be an oversimplification to explain the Arab world 's decline solely through the Arab-Israeli conflict . Other factors including the nature of post-independence states , economic structures , weak institutions , foreign intervention , and internal political divisions also played significant roles . The history of the modern Arab world is therefore best understood as the product of multiple interacting forces rather than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ On the Theory of the Decline of Arab Societies : Reassessments in Modern Arab History . @@138684632 <p> Sumana Roy translates Jagadish Chandra Bose 's revolutionary writings on plant sentience and communication . Jagadish Chandra Bose ( 1858-1937 ) was a Bengali scientist and polymath who developed a theory of plant communication more than a century ago . Bose suggested that plants had their own vocabulary , an " unvoiced life " that he recorded as a " script " with a crescograph , a device that measured how plants respond to each other and their environments . Since taking charge of the national team in 2024 , the former striker has repeatedly portrayed Egypt 's football successes as inseparable from the country 's political leadership . <p> After Egypt qualified for the World @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ top of the pyramid , " saying the greatest reward he sought was an opportunity to meet the president . Match tickets are sold exclusively through Tazkarti , a platform requiring biometric fan registration and operated by a subsidiary of United Media Services , a media conglomerate linked to Egypt 's General Intelligence Service , The Guardian report further added . <p> Other subsidiaries oversee television broadcasting , commercial rights , stadium management and even official World Cup fan zones . @@138741766 <h> The Manufacture of Impunity : Gaza , Lebanon , and the Architecture of a State 's Violence <h> How a Political Apparatus Secures Its Crimes and Captures American Power <p> The bodies of twin 9-year-old brothers Moaz and Moataz , who were killed in Israeli airstrikes that killed at least 60 civilians overnight , are carried at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis , southern Gaza Strip , on 15 May 2025 . ( Doaa Albaz/ActiveStills ) <p> A thousand days . <p> Say it slowly , because Gaza no longer can . A thousand dawns over a strip of land smaller than a city , each one breaking not upon rooftops but upon their absence . A thousand nights beneath the same drone that does not sleep , does not blink , does not forgive . There , time is no longer counted in seasons , or harvests , or the growth of children -- it is counted in funerals , and in the funerals that could not be held , for want of hands to dig . <p> A thousand days , and the arithmetic is unbearable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and seventy-three thousand wounded , nine and a half thousand more still folded into the concrete , waiting for hands that will not come . More than half of them women , the old , the very small . Twenty-one thousand of them children -- a generation entered into a ledger before it could learn to read one . And twelve thousand pregnancies lost -- miscarried or ended under starvation and the ruin of the hospitals : a people struck at the root , before breath . <p> They killed the ones who film it -- two hundred and sixty-two journalists . They killed the ones who dig for the living -- a hundred and forty-five rescuers , seventeen hundred healers . They did not merely wage a war . They made a method of it -- and the world , for a thousand days , agreed to call the method by another name . <p> This is not about a people , a religion , or a supposed nature . It is about a state , a specific government , and the machinery that has kept its crimes running @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ precisely -- and the thousand days become an indictment that no delay at The Hague , no veto in New York , no bomb out of Washington can any longer disguise . <p> In 2026 the question is no longer whether crimes are being committed . An unprecedented convergence of independent bodies has settled that . The question is by what mechanism a state commits them in full view , theorizes them , replicates them from one theater to the next , and secures the guarantee of the world 's foremost power . That is the machinery to dismantle . <p> The Crime Named <p> The turning point is not rhetorical . It is juridical . On 16 September 2025 , the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry -- chaired by Navi Pillay , former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and former judge of the International Criminal Court -- concluded that the State of Israel is committing genocide in Gaza ( report A/HRC/60/CRP.3 ) . The Commission found four of the five acts defined in Article II of the 1948 Convention : killing ; serious bodily or mental harm @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ destroy the group ; and measures intended to prevent births -- the axis I have called reprocide . <p> What makes the report decisive is that it clears the hardest threshold in criminal law : intent -- dolus specialis , the specific intent to destroy a group as such . Applying the " only reasonable inference " standard the ICJ set in Bosnia v. Serbia , the Commission holds that the statements of Israel 's highest authorities are direct evidence of that intent . It names Prime Minister Netanyahu , President Herzog , and former Defense Minister Gallant . On 9 October 2023 , announcing the total siege , Gallant said : " We are fighting human animals and we are acting accordingly . " Some insist he meant only combatants . The immediate context -- no water , no food , no electricity , no fuel , for 2.3 million people -- led the Commission , and many jurists , to read it as the marking of an entire population . <p> The finding does not stand alone . It sits in a chain . The ICJ , seized @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ harm was " plausible " and ordered provisional measures . Amnesty International concluded genocide in December 2024 . The International Association of Genocide Scholars did the same in August 2025 . In November 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant -- for crimes against humanity and war crimes , including starvation as a method of warfare . In its advisory opinion of 19 July 2024 , the ICJ had already declared the occupation unlawful . <p> Honesty requires stating what these bodies did not say . The ICJ has not ruled on the merits ; the case will run at least until 2029 . The label " genocide " remains legally contested : serious jurists see war crimes and crimes against humanity without , in their view , the specific intent being met . And Israel offers a defense coherent on its own terms : a war of self-defense after the 7 October 2023 massacre -- roughly 1,200 dead , some 250 hostages -- against an organization that deliberately embeds itself in the civilian fabric . <p> These facts are real , and it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ None of them authorizes the siege of an entire population , the methodical destruction of the health system , the forced displacement of nearly the whole territory , or the diversion of aid -- a " facade , " the Commission calls it -- masking a policy of starvation . As of 4 July 2026 , Gaza 's Health Ministry records more than 73,000 dead and more than 173,000 wounded since October 2023 , figures Israel disputes . Here Achille Mbembe 's concept applies without strain : not the power to make live , but necropolitics -- the sovereign power to designate who is disposable and to administer death as an instrument of government . <p> The Engine <p> A crime of state has a genealogy . Israel 's current government is where two long-separate currents have fused . <p> The first is the Revisionist Zionism of Vladimir Jabotinsky -- the secular , nationalist matrix of which Netanyahu is the direct heir ; his father Benzion was Jabotinsky 's secretary . Its doctrine , the " iron wall , " holds that only a force the native population can never @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of raw leverage and territorial maximalism . <p> The second is Kahanism , the eliminationist eschatology of Rabbi Meir Kahane , whose Kach party was designated a terrorist organization and banned . Its institutional heir , Itamar Ben-Gvir -- Minister of National Security , convicted of incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organization , who for years displayed in his home a portrait of Baruch Goldstein , the Hebron massacre perpetrator -- has carried that ideology from banned terrorism to sovereign power . Beside him , Bezalel Smotrich embodies the messianic , settler wing . <p> The decisive fact is that Netanyahu , a secular Revisionist , was the vehicle of this normalization . It was he who , to survive politically , engineered the 2021 -- 2022 merger that brought these currents into government . His responsibility is not doctrinal but instrumental -- which is precisely what makes it indefensible . The cynical strategist and the messianic fanatic found each other . <p> This convergence produces the language that becomes , before the courts , evidence of intent . When ministers call for erasure , deportation , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are documenting a project . But distinguish , as a scrupulous analyst must : this project is condemned by a large part of the Jewish and rabbinic world itself , whose highest authorities denounced its supremacist texts as racist . It is an identifiable political current , not a people , that captured the machinery of state . That precision is your strength . <p> The Method <p> What unfolds in Lebanon reveals a doctrine , not excess -- an openly avowed military theory of disproportion . <p> The Dahiya doctrine , formulated after 2006 and named for the Beirut suburb leveled that year , prescribes massive , disproportionate force and the deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure to impose lasting " deterrence . " In law , that is the definition of collective punishment : a war crime elevated into a method . <p> The application was methodical . In September 2024 , the booby-trapped pager operation -- thousands of explosives hidden in communication devices , detonated at once -- killed some forty people , civilians among them , and wounded roughly four thousand . It was indiscriminate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ device at the instant of detonation . Then came the assassination of Hassan Nasrallah , under more than eighty bombs , including US-made 2,000-pound bunker-busters , in a residential district . The 2024 war killed , per Lebanon 's Health Ministry , about 2,720 people in Lebanon -- most of them civilians -- and displaced more than 1.2 million . <p> The November 2024 ceasefire proved a fiction . UNIFIL documented more than ten thousand Israeli violations . Strikes continued " almost daily , " killing hundreds during the truce . Israel refused to withdraw fully , keeping five positions on Lebanese soil . Then , in 2026 , under cover of the war on Iran , the escalation resumed and the mask fell . In March , Minister Smotrich threatened to bombard Beirut 's southern suburbs until they resemble Khan Younis -- the Gaza city all but erased . The doctrine no longer hides . It advertises itself as an exportable model . <p> Probity demands the other side . Hezbollah opened fire on northern Israel on 8 October 2023 , violated the truce by rebuilding its arsenal , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . They do not turn a documented collective punishment into a lawful act of war -- which is exactly the confusion the Dahiya doctrine is built to install . <p> The Design <p> Gaza and Lebanon are not separate episodes . They are faces of one design : the pursuit of a strategic monopoly -- permanent military supremacy and the methodical neutralization of any actor capable of contesting it . <p> This grid explains the 2026 sequence : the war on Iran , the assassination of the Supreme Leader , the fragmentation of what Tehran called the " Axis of Resistance . " Hamas decapitated , Hezbollah stripped of its command , the Syrian corridor collapsed . Add the territorial creep : positions held in south Lebanon , the persistent occupation of the Golan , the annexationist drive in the West Bank . Justice Without Exception : Palestinianism and the Global Call for Disarmament <p> PALESTINIANISM AS AN ANALYTICAL FRAMEWORK <p> Across these six articles , Palestinianism is developed as an interpretive framework for examining how human dignity is distributed , protected , or withheld under contemporary international order . It is not an identity label or a political slogan . It is a diagnostic lens for identifying structural patterns of vulnerability and protection . The framework focuses on how humanitarian norms are articulated as universal while applied selectively in practice . <p> Three core dimensions define Palestinianism . <p> First , structural vulnerability : the persistent exposure of certain populations to harm even when legal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ incidental outcome of conflict , but as a predictable condition shaped by political context and enforcement gaps . <p> Second , normalization of harm : the gradual institutional and public desensitization to recurring civilian suffering . When harm becomes routine , the urgency of intervention declines , and violations lose their exceptional character . <p> Third , accountability asymmetry : the uneven application of international humanitarian norms depending on geopolitical alignment , institutional capacity , and political will . This asymmetry produces a credibility gap between legal universality and operational reality . <p> Methodologically , Palestinianism does not replace legal adjudication or empirical reporting . Instead , it interrogates the structural conditions under which these systems operate inconsistently . It asks why protection is activated in some contexts and delayed or absent in others , and how these patterns shape the lived experience of civilians . <p> THE UN COMMISSION REPORT AS EMPIRICAL STRESS TEST <p> The June 23 , 2026 report of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory , including East Jerusalem , and Israel , titled : <p> " The essence of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Palestinian children in the Occupied Palestinian Territory since 7 October 2023 " <p> provides a significant empirical reference point for evaluating the explanatory scope of Palestinianism . <p> The report documents extensive civilian harm in Gaza and the wider occupied territory , including the deliberate killing , maiming , starvation , and terrorization of Palestinian children . It identifies patterns of conduct amounting to war crimes , crimes against humanity , and acts of genocide . It also describes systemic mechanisms through which harm to children became predictable , widespread , and institutionally tolerated . <p> The significance of the report extends beyond legal classification . Its analytical value lies in documenting persistent civilian vulnerability in a context where legal protections formally exist but operational outcomes remain uneven . This aligns directly with the structural concerns raised in Palestinianism . <p> From the perspective of Palestinianism , the report functions as a stress test . It demonstrates a recurring condition in which normative universality exists at the level of law but is inconsistently translated into protection in practice . The documented civilian harm illustrates how structural vulnerability , normalization of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> COMPETING INTERPRETATIONS <p> The interpretation advanced here is not exclusive . A legalist reading would emphasize the provisional nature of commission findings and the requirement of judicial adjudication before definitive conclusions regarding intent or responsibility . A security-centered interpretation would frame civilian harm within asymmetric warfare , operational complexity , and contested battlefield environments . <p> Palestinianism does not reject these interpretations . Instead , it operates at a different level of analysis . It examines systemic patterns of protection and vulnerability across international order , regardless of intent attribution in individual cases . Its focus is not on adjudicating events , but on identifying structural regularities in how humanitarian norms are applied and constrained . <p> SYSTEMIC INSIGHT AND IMPLICATIONS <p> A central proposition of Palestinianism is that repeated documentation of civilian harm without effective enforcement produces a structural credibility gap in humanitarian governance . The June 2026 UN Commission report reinforces three systemic dynamics . <p> Third , temporal asymmetry : the pace of violence often exceeds the pace of accountability , creating a persistent gap between harm and remedy . <p> These dynamics are not anomalies @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ political fragmentation and uneven enforcement capacity . <p> CONCLUSION <p> The June 23 , 2026 UN Commission report provides a significant empirical reference in debates on civilian protection . Palestinianism offers an interpretive lens that situates these findings within a broader analysis of global humanitarian governance . The central question is structural : under what conditions do universal humanitarian norms fail to produce universal protection ? Addressing this requires attention not only to violations , but to the systemic mechanisms that determine when protection is activated , delayed , or absent . @@138772476 <p> Anyone following Israel 's military campaigns in Palestine and Lebanon will notice a recurring pattern : residential neighborhoods reduced to rubble , thousands of families left homeless , and entire communities requiring years to rebuild . With every new round of conflict , the same question resurfaces : why do homes occupy such a central place in Israel 's military operations ? <p> The official Israeli position is that its strikes target military infrastructure or locations allegedly used by armed groups , including weapons depots , command centers , or rocket-launching sites . From a military perspective , attacking legitimate military objectives may be lawful under international humanitarian law , provided that the principles of distinction , proportionality , and precaution are respected . <p> However , the scale of destruction witnessed in Palestinian and Lebanese communities over the years has led many legal experts and human rights organizations to question whether every demolition can genuinely be justified by military necessity , or whether some operations go beyond that threshold , inflicting widespread harm on civilians and civilian infrastructure . <p> A home is far more than a concrete @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and economic stability . When thousands of homes are destroyed , the consequences extend far beyond property loss . Families are displaced , education is disrupted , livelihoods collapse , and communities are fragmented . These effects often endure long after the fighting has ended . <p> Some analysts argue that , beyond their declared military objectives , large-scale demolitions may also serve broader strategic purposes . These may include increasing pressure on the social environment in which armed groups operate , reducing their operational freedom , or imposing significant costs on communities affected by the conflict . In certain contexts , observers have also debated whether extensive destruction could influence long-term demographic or urban realities . Such interpretations remain the subject of political , legal , and academic debate rather than settled fact . <p> In the Palestinian territories , another dimension emerges through administrative and punitive house demolitions . Human rights organizations have criticized these practices , arguing that when the consequences fall upon family members who were not involved in any violent act , they may amount to collective punishment , which is prohibited under international @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are intended to deter future attacks and enhance public security . <p> The most profound consequence of home demolitions is not merely the number of buildings reduced to rubble , but the lasting psychological impact they leave on entire societies . Cities can be rebuilt , but restoring a sense of safety , belonging , and trust is far more difficult . Every demolished home represents a family whose life has been fundamentally altered . <p> Decades of conflict have repeatedly demonstrated that military force can destroy buildings within moments , yet it is far less capable of resolving the political grievances and historical disputes that sustain prolonged conflicts . Rubble may erase structures , but it rarely eliminates the underlying causes of violence . <p> For that reason , the continued destruction of residential areas raises questions not only about military effectiveness but also about the long-term humanitarian , legal , and political costs of such a strategy . As civilian suffering increases , so too does the need to ensure that all parties to armed conflicts comply with international humanitarian law and uphold their obligations to protect civilians @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the number of buildings destroyed , but by whether they bring societies any closer to a just and lasting peace . As long as homes continue to become battlefields , every military victory will remain overshadowed by the human cost left behind . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Husein Mahmoud Saleh is an independent writer and political analyst specializing in Middle Eastern affairs , with a particular focus on human rights , conflict , forced displacement , and regional politics . @@138791513 <h> The weaponisation of the UN <p> By Manjari Singh <p> As the war in Gaza continues to divide global opinion , a new United Nations report accusing Israel of grave violations against Palestinian children has reignited questions not only about accountability , but also about the credibility and consistency of international institutions <p> Two developments this week show how readily the great powers and multilateral institutions will settle the fate of another conflict in the Middle East . At Lake Lucerne , the United States and Iran agreed a roadmap to wind down the war in Lebanon and built a mechanism to govern the fighting between Israel and Hezbollah , while Israel itself was given no seat at the table . <p> In Geneva , the UN Human Rights Council received a report accusing Israel of the gravest crimes in international law over its conduct towards the children of Gaza . India holds no stake in either battlefield , yet has reason to watch how this second judgment was reached . <p> The death of a child is the heaviest sorrow a society can carry , and that it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hold . A child killed in Gaza is an irreplaceable world ended ; so is a child in Tel Aviv , or on a road in the Kashmir Valley . To ask how a child died , and at whose hand , is the seriousness that might protect the next one . <p> There is another moral question that deserves reflection in India . The massacres of October 7 , in which Israeli civilians , including children , were murdered , kidnapped and brutalised , marked the beginning of this war . Yet many voices that now speak with certainty about Israel 's conduct had little or nothing to say when those atrocities occurred . Moral concern can not be selective . A standard that condemns civilian suffering only after one side responds , while remaining silent when the violence that triggered the conflict is unleashed , diminishes its own credibility . One may criticise Israel 's actions and still recognise that any serious moral accounting of this war must begin with October 7 . To omit that starting point is not impartiality ; it is incompleteness . <p> In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ UN High Commissioner for Human Rights issued reports on Jammu and Kashmir that New Delhi rejected as fallacious , tendentious and motivated . The objection was never that Kashmiri suffering was unreal ; no honest Indian would say so . The objection was to the UN system . A UN office had assembled unverified figures , relied on interested testimony , set aside the long history of cross-border terrorism , and pronounced a confident verdict on a place it had no standing to judge . Governments in Delhi of every stripe have held that line since . <p> That is the lens through which the Gaza report deserves to be read . This Commission is the only standing body in the UN system aimed permanently at a single country , created by a resolution that half the Council declined to support . It rests its conclusions on testimony it can not independently verify and , in places , on its own previous reports ; it reaches determinations on ballistics and military operations for which it has no evident expertise , then dresses them as legal findings , though it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the accused state ten days to answer a hundred-page document covering three years of war . None of this certifies Israel 's account of any single incident . But the report 's central claims are precisely the kind an impartial process would treat as contested rather than settled . <p> Much turns on disputed ground . The Commission 's own reports have not kept their ratios of children to combatants consistent . Its treatment of schools and hospitals sets aside a documented pattern of armed groups operating from within civilian sites , the fact that decides whether a strike was a crime or a tragedy of war : weapons recovered from a kindergarten , a tunnel shaft beneath an infant 's cot , an attack on the Al-Taba'een site that the report lists without recording that the building had become a base for militants . The account of the Al-Ahli hospital explosion , attributed to Israel within hours , was later contradicted by American , British and Canadian assessments pointing to a misfired Palestinian rocket . <p> On starvation , the report passes over the more than a million children @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the diversion of humanitarian aid by the armed groups themselves . One need not settle any of these to see the difficulty : Each judgment falls the same way , against the accused , and a tribunal whose every doubt resolves in one direction is not weighing evidence . It is ratifying a verdict it brought with it . <p> There is also a distinction that should matter to a democracy . A democracy carries the means of its own correction : courts that rule against the government , a free press , an electorate that removes it . Israel , whatever one concludes about its conduct , has these institutions ; the armed movements arrayed against it offer their people none . <p> Candour is owed about the forum doing the judging . The human-rights machinery of the United Nations carries a long and uneven record , having seated serial abusers on its councils and trained a permanent focus on one democracy while openly repressive states drew little notice . Such a body has not earned the authority to pronounce final verdicts on a sovereign nation , and the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the dock . Accountability imposed from outside , on evidence a state was never allowed to test , only imitates the rule of law . <p> This is the pattern India must recognise , because it was once turned against India itself . A standing body , insulated from accountability , selects a single sovereign state , assembles a record it does not let that state test , and converts a political campaign into the language of law and its gravest charges . The instrument is the human-rights report ; the purpose is the weaponisation of the United Nations against an unfavourable state . <p> Verdicts handed down from Geneva harden the warring and embolden those who profit from grievance ; they have never stopped a war or returned a child to a parent . Peace is made by states willing to talk , and made faster when the world resists anointing permanent villains and victims . India 's instinct , shaped by its own experience , has favoured dialogue over denunciation . @@138834556 <h> Beyond the " Muslim NATO " - Strategic Autonomy in a Multipolar World <h> " Muslim NATO " is a political expression for an emerging regional defence bloc centred around Turkey , Saudi Arabia , and Pakistan . Built upon a strategic mutual defence agreement established between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia , this framework mirrors NATO 's Article 5 by dictating that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all . <p> The phrase " Muslim NATO " has begun to touch geo-politics with increasing frequency in diplomatic commentary , think-tank discussions and sections of the international media . It evokes images of a military alliance forged along religious lines , mirroring the North Atlantic Treaty Organization . The phrase is provocative , but it is also misleading . There is no formal military pact binding Muslim-majority nations into a unified defence structure comparable to NATO . Yet dismissing the discussion altogether would be equally mistaken . Something important is unfolding across West Asia and the wider Islamic world . What is emerging is not a religious alliance but the gradual search for a new security @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ realities of an increasingly multipolar world . When old alliances lose legitimacy , new partnerships emerge -- not necessarily to wage war , but to reclaim the right to shape their own destiny . <p> This development can not be understood in isolation . It is inseparable from the erosion of the unipolar order that emerged after the Cold War . For nearly three decades , the United States and its Western allies enjoyed unparalleled military , political and financial dominance . NATO expanded , interventions multiplied and Washington increasingly assumed the role of global arbiter . The promise was that Western leadership would deliver stability , democracy and prosperity . <p> The record tells a different story . <p> From Afghanistan to Iraq , from Libya to Syria , interventions justified in the name of freedom often left fractured societies , weakened institutions and prolonged instability . The costs were borne overwhelmingly by ordinary people . The promise of a rules-based international order increasingly appeared selective , applied rigorously to adversaries but often suspended when strategic allies violated the very principles the West claimed to uphold . <p> Nowhere @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Israel 's devastating military campaign in Gaza , backed politically and militarily by major Western powers despite mounting international criticism , has transformed perceptions across the Global South . For many governments and millions of citizens , Gaza has become the defining symbol of an international order in which international law is invoked inconsistently and humanitarian principles are subordinated to geopolitical interests . <p> The consequences extend well beyond Palestine . The war has accelerated a broader reassessment of global alliances . Countries that once relied almost exclusively on Western security guarantees have begun asking difficult questions . Can security continue to depend upon external powers whose strategic priorities frequently shift ? Can sovereignty be protected when regional conflicts become theatres for global competition ? Can lasting peace emerge from endless militarisation directed from outside the region ? <p> These questions are driving profound changes . <p> The Middle East has traditionally been portrayed as a region defined by immutable rivalries : Sunni versus Shia , Arab versus Persian , monarchies versus republics . Such divisions undoubtedly exist and have fuelled painful conflicts . Yet they have often been magnified @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Divided neighbours are easier to manage than confident partners capable of defining their own collective interests . <p> Recent diplomacy suggests another possibility . The restoration of relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran , facilitated by China rather than Washington , was more than a bilateral breakthrough . It symbolised a growing willingness among regional powers to resolve disputes through dialogue instead of perpetual confrontation . Similar efforts to rebuild relations among former rivals indicate a recognition that endless hostility has exhausted political capital while delivering little security . <p> This does not mean that deep differences have disappeared . National interests continue to diverge , ideological disagreements remain sharp and regional competition has not ended . But governments increasingly recognise that cooperation in selected areas may serve their interests better than permanent confrontation . <p> This emerging pragmatism has coincided with broader transformations in global politics . The expansion of BRICS , growing trade conducted outside the US dollar , renewed South-South cooperation and increasing resistance to unilateral sanctions all point towards the diffusion of global power . States across Asia , Africa and Latin America are seeking greater @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Security naturally forms part of this larger search for autonomy . <p> Western analysts often interpret greater military coordination among Muslim-majority countries primarily through the lens of political Islam . Such interpretations deserve careful scrutiny . They frequently assume that any institutional cooperation involving Muslim states must necessarily be ideological or anti-Western . Yet similar assumptions are rarely applied elsewhere . European military cooperation is not described as a " Christian alliance . " Regional defence arrangements in Asia are seldom interpreted through religious identity . The label " Muslim NATO " therefore reveals as much about Western anxieties as it does about developments within the Islamic world . <p> Religion alone can not explain the changing strategic landscape . States act primarily according to national interests , economic priorities and security calculations . Shared religious identity may facilitate dialogue , but it is seldom sufficient to sustain long-term geopolitical cooperation . History offers abundant evidence that Muslim-majority countries have often disagreed as intensely with one another as they have with non-Muslim states . <p> Equally important is the need to distinguish Islam from the actions of violent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Every major religious tradition has produced movements that distort faith for political or violent ends . Christianity witnessed the Crusades , the Inquisition and contemporary forms of white supremacist extremism invoking Christian symbolism . Hindu nationalism , Buddhist militancy in Myanmar and extremist Jewish settler movements demonstrate that religious intolerance is not unique to Islam . It is therefore analytically flawed and morally indefensible to equate the faith of nearly two billion Muslims with the ideology of fringe organisations . <p> Indeed , many Muslim-majority societies have themselves been the principal victims of extremist violence . Their governments have devoted immense resources to combating terrorism while simultaneously confronting external intervention , economic sanctions and internal political pressures . To understand current efforts at regional cooperation solely through the prism of radical Islam is therefore to misunderstand both history and contemporary geopolitics . <p> The more persuasive explanation lies elsewhere . A growing number of states have concluded that dependence upon external security providers has failed to deliver durable peace . Decades of foreign military presence have not prevented war . Arms purchases have not eliminated insecurity . Proxy conflicts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , governments are exploring whether regional problems require regional solutions . <p> It is against this background that discussions of a so-called " Muslim NATO " acquire their real significance -- not as evidence of an ideological crusade , but as an expression of a wider search for strategic independence in a changing international order . <p> Muslim NATO ? Divided neighbours are easier to manage than confident partners capable of defining their own collective interests . <p> Recent diplomacy suggests another possibility @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , facilitated by China rather than Washington , was more than a bilateral breakthrough . It symbolised a growing willingness among regional powers to resolve disputes through dialogue instead of perpetual confrontation . Similar efforts to rebuild relations among former rivals indicate a recognition that endless hostility has exhausted political capital while delivering little security . <p> This does not mean that deep differences have disappeared . National interests continue to diverge , ideological disagreements remain sharp and regional competition has not ended . But governments increasingly recognise that cooperation in selected areas may serve their interests better than permanent confrontation . <p> This emerging pragmatism has coincided with broader transformations in global politics . The expansion of BRICS , growing trade conducted outside the US dollar , renewed South-South cooperation and increasing resistance to unilateral sanctions all point towards the diffusion of global power . States across Asia , Africa and Latin America are seeking greater strategic flexibility rather than exclusive dependence on any single bloc . <p> Security naturally forms part of this larger search for autonomy . <p> Western analysts often interpret greater military coordination among Muslim-majority @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ interpretations deserve careful scrutiny . They frequently assume that any institutional cooperation involving Muslim states must necessarily be ideological or anti-Western . Yet similar assumptions are rarely applied elsewhere . European military cooperation is not described as a " Christian alliance . " Regional defence arrangements in Asia are seldom interpreted through religious identity . The label " Muslim NATO " therefore reveals as much about Western anxieties as it does about developments within the Islamic world . <p> Religion alone can not explain the changing strategic landscape . States act primarily according to national interests , economic priorities and security calculations . Shared religious identity may facilitate dialogue , but it is seldom sufficient to sustain long-term geopolitical cooperation . History offers abundant evidence that Muslim-majority countries have often disagreed as intensely with one another as they have with non-Muslim states . <p> Equally important is the need to distinguish Islam from the actions of violent extremist organisations that have claimed to act in its name . Every major religious tradition has produced movements that distort faith for political or violent ends . Christianity witnessed the Crusades , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ symbolism . Hindu nationalism , Buddhist militancy in Myanmar and extremist Jewish settler movements demonstrate that religious intolerance is not unique to Islam . It is therefore analytically flawed and morally indefensible to equate the faith of nearly two billion Muslims with the ideology of fringe organisations . <p> Indeed , many Muslim-majority societies have themselves been the principal victims of extremist violence . Their governments have devoted immense resources to combating terrorism while simultaneously confronting external intervention , economic sanctions and internal political pressures . To understand current efforts at regional cooperation solely through the prism of radical Islam is therefore to misunderstand both history and contemporary geopolitics . <p> The more persuasive explanation lies elsewhere . A growing number of states have concluded that dependence upon external security providers has failed to deliver durable peace . Decades of foreign military presence have not prevented war . Arms purchases have not eliminated insecurity . Proxy conflicts have enriched defence industries while devastating entire societies . Increasingly , governments are exploring whether regional problems require regional solutions . <p> It is against this background that discussions of a so-called " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ evidence of an ideological crusade , but as an expression of a wider search for strategic independence in a changing international order . <p> Empires are built on fear . Enduring alliances are built on trust . If a Muslim NATO is to mean anything , it must reject the first and embody the second . Otherwise , it will merely become another chapter in the long history of militarised politics . This is not to suggest Iran has abandoned Palestinian groups . " Whether or not Iranian leaders would describe their policy this way , recent events closely resemble this logic . <p> If Iran truly regarded Palestine as its foremost regional priority , one would expect Tehran to insist that broader regional understandings include meaningful pressure to reduce Israeli military operations in Gaza or secure humanitarian and political concessions for Palestinians . Instead , Iran has consistently focused negotiations on sanctions , nuclear issues , regional influence , and deterrence . <p> Perhaps no episode illustrates this contradiction more vividly than the killing of Hamas political chief Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran in 2024 . The episode underscored that Iran 's strategic calculus remained centered on its own security rather than Palestinian objectives . <p> Iran 's strongest regional partner has always been Hezbollah . Unlike Hamas , Hezbollah provides strategic depth on Israel 's northern border and serves as a key pillar of Iran 's deterrence strategy . Palestinian groups , by contrast , have often functioned as instruments of broader regional influence rather than ends in themselves . <p> Like most states , Iran ultimately prioritises survival over ideology . Despite decades of revolutionary rhetoric , its leaders calculate costs , assess risks , and avoid actions that could threaten regime survival . That explains why Iran has avoided a full-scale war with Israel over Gaza despite repeated declarations of solidarity with Palestinians . From a realist perspective , this is unsurprising . From the standpoint of Iran 's revolutionary narrative , however , it exposes an uncomfortable inconsistency . <p> Iran also faces a credibility challenge . Its ideological commitment and long-standing ties with Palestinian factions remain genuine . But the evidence suggests that Iran 's support has clear limits . It is prepared to back Palestinians only so long as doing so does not fundamentally endanger its own strategic interests . The broader lesson is familiar in international politics . Governments often speak the language of solidarity and resistance , but when strategic survival collides with ideological commitment , states almost always choose survival . Palestine , once again , finds itself caught between powerful narratives and even more powerful national interests . ( IANS )

@@138890792 <h> Gaza After the War : When Survival Becomes a Daily Struggle <p> A war may end with a political declaration , but for the people of Gaza , war does not end when the guns fall silent . It continues through siege , rubble , hunger , disease , displacement , and the collapse of the very foundations of human life . Death does not always come from a missile ; sometimes it comes from the absence of medicine , the lack of clean water , the delay of humanitarian aid , or a hospital no longer capable of saving a dying child . <p> International humanitarian law was created to protect civilians in the darkest moments of armed conflict , not to remain a collection of legal texts cited at conferences while millions are left to endure unbearable suffering . The Geneva Conventions impose clear obligations on parties to a conflict to protect civilians , prohibit collective punishment , and facilitate the rapid and unimpeded delivery of humanitarian assistance . International human rights law likewise recognizes every person 's inherent rights to life , food , water , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ civilians are denied these fundamental rights after the cessation of hostilities , the issue is no longer merely a humanitarian crisis . It becomes a profound test of the international community 's commitment to the rule of law and the universal principles of justice . <p> Today , the people of Gaza are not asking for luxury or privilege . They are asking for the minimum conditions that international law guarantees to every human being : for a father to find bread for his children , for a mother to obtain medicine for her sick child , for displaced families to sleep under a roof instead of beneath torn tents , for the wounded to receive treatment in functioning hospitals , and for children to return to classrooms instead of growing up among ruins . <p> Any continued restrictions that unnecessarily impede humanitarian relief or delay the reconstruction of civilian infrastructure deepen human suffering and jeopardize the future of an entire society . Every day that civilians are deprived of essential necessities leaves physical and psychological scars that may endure for generations , creating a generation that has learned the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of peace . <p> Under the fundamental principles of international humanitarian law , civilians must never become instruments of political or military pressure . They are not parties to the conflict and must not bear the consequences of decisions they did not make or battles they did not choose . Human dignity is not a privilege granted by governments or military powers ; it is an inherent right that does not disappear in times of war and can not be suspended for political convenience . <p> The responsibility of the international community extends far beyond calling for a ceasefire . It includes ensuring compliance with international law , facilitating the rapid and safe delivery of humanitarian assistance , supporting the reconstruction of civilian infrastructure , and ensuring accountability for serious violations of international humanitarian law through appropriate legal mechanisms . <p> Justice can not be measured by the number of diplomatic statements issued , but by the number of lives that are protected . Law loses its purpose if it can not safeguard the hungry child , the patient waiting for medicine , or the family forced to live on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that the world possessed an extensive legal framework designed to protect civilians during armed conflict . The question future generations will ask is whether there was sufficient political will to enforce those protections when Gaza needed them most . Laws that fail to protect human beings in their most vulnerable moments lose their moral purpose , and humanity that remains silent in the face of immense civilian suffering risks becoming little more than a slogan rather than a universal value . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Husein Mahmoud Saleh is an independent writer and political analyst specializing in Middle Eastern affairs , with a particular focus on human rights , conflict , forced displacement , and regional politics .
