It is a genuine settlement no predecessor achieved . It also sits oddly next to Ankara 's reported success , described this year in Israeli press accounts , in persuading Donald Trump to shelve a Mossad-backed plan to arm Kurdish militias against Iran . Whether the fighters in question are burning weapons in Sulaymaniyah or being organized by Israeli intelligence , Turkey 's answer to Kurdish paramilitary power has been the same : neutralize it , by whatever means the moment allows . <p> Foreign policy runs on the same instinct for turning constraint into leverage . The pro-Kurdish DEM party holds 56 - exactly the kind of bloc a movement freshly persuaded to lay down its weapons might be willing to lend the president who ended its war . @@139138035 <h> The Speck , the Log , and the Larger Arsenal : A Response to " The Dangerous Theology Behind Iran 's Nuclear Ambitions " <p> There is a well-known teaching of Jesus Christ of Nazareth : that a person should not busy himself removing the speck from his brother 's eye while a log remains lodged in his own ( Matthew 7:3 -- 5 ) . The teaching is usually read as counsel against personal hypocrisy . But there is a second , more political misuse to which it is regularly put , and it is this misuse that the article under review , " The Dangerous Theology Behind Iran 's Nuclear Ambitions , " exemplifies with unusual clarity . The misuse works as follows : a writer takes the most extravagant , least representative statement available from a rival civilisation , treats it as though it defined that civilisation entire , and sets it beside an idealised self-portrait of his own tradition , scrubbed of its own extremists , its own accelerationists , and its own theologically sanctioned violence . The speck in the other 's eye is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The log in one 's own eye is simply not mentioned , on the unstated assumption that one 's own tradition does not grow logs . <p> This is not a marginal rhetorical flourish . It is , this response will argue , the master technique of tribalist othering , and it is dangerous precisely because it inverts the ethical instruction from which it borrows its imagery . Jesus 's teaching was meant to produce humility and self-scrutiny before judgement of the neighbour . Deployed as the article deploys it -- implicitly , through a set of " faith facts " about a rival civilisation 's supernatural claims , set against a description of " Christian hope " that mentions none of Christian history 's own apocalyptic violence -- the same imagery produces the opposite of humility . It produces a permission slip . It tells the reader : your side sees clearly ; theirs is blind and dangerous . That is not the ethic of Matthew 7 . It is the ethic of Matthew 7 turned inside out and worn as a mask . <p> This response draws @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ extreme Twelver Shi'ism , radical Christian Zionism , and radical Jewish religious Zionism side by side . That study is explicit that it does not rank the three traditions against one another , and that the danger it identifies in each is a minority hermeneutic , not a demographic reality . This response puts the same material to a narrower and more polemical use than the study itself attempts : to show , point by point , that the article 's argument fails on its own terms once the same evidentiary standard is applied symmetrically , and to argue further that where genuinely dangerous accelerationist theology does exist within the American and Israeli political mainstream , its danger is of a different order of magnitude -- because it sits inside the command structure of the most powerful military machine in the world and its most heavily armed regional client , rather than inside a heavily sanctioned regional power with a fraction of that reach . <p> Methodological Objection : Comparing Best to Worst <p> Begin with method , because the article 's method is the whole of its argument . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about a supernatural experience reported by a former president twenty years ago ; a general statement that " Iranian leaders " follow a radical Mahdist interpretation of prophecy ; and an assertion that understanding this " apocalyptic worldview " is critical for American Christians . From these three claims it proceeds , within a handful of paragraphs , to a picture of " Iran 's leadership " as a monolithic bloc animated by a single , uniform , and irrational theology , oriented toward manufactured chaos as a matter of settled doctrine . <p> Compare this with how the article treats its own tradition . " Christians are called to be peace-makers , to pray for our enemies , and to trust in God 's sovereignty over human history , " it states , without qualification , without reference to any Christian who has ever believed otherwise , and without so much as a subordinate clause acknowledging that tens of millions of American Christians belong to networks that teach a starkly different , action-oriented eschatology , in which peace treaties are labelled satanic deceptions and territorial compromise is apostasy ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ dispensationalism in its politically organised form -- in detail : a " woodenly literal hermeneutic , " in the words of its own proponents , that reads modern geopolitics as a real-time instalment of a fixed prophetic script . The article 's author does not deny that this tradition exists . The author simply does not mention it , because mentioning it would collapse the binary on which the whole essay depends . <p> This is the practice of comparing " our " best with " their " worst named at the outset of this response , and it is worth stating plainly why it is dangerous rather than merely unfair . It is dangerous because it launders a policy conclusion -- support a " strong American defence posture , " treat diplomacy with Tehran as inherently naive -- through a theological argument that has been immunised against its own tradition 's counter-evidence . A reader who accepts the article 's method has no tools left with which to evaluate accelerationist theology when it appears , as this response will show that it does appear , inside the very alliance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ There is a second methodological defect worth naming before turning to specific points . The article treats " understanding this apocalyptic worldview " as a matter of pure description -- an act of neutral religious literacy offered to help American Christians " comprehend the religious motivations driving Iranian actions . " But description is never neutral once it becomes asymmetric . A profile that describes only one party 's theology , and only that party 's most extreme adherents , does not inform a reader 's judgement ; it pre-loads it . By the time the article reaches its policy conclusion -- standing " with Israel , " supporting " a strong American defence posture " -- the reader has already been given every reason to trust one side 's motives and none to question the other 's . This is the precise operation that the comparative study describes as typological branding : the transformation of a political rival into an ontological category , " the false messiah driving Iran 's revolutionary regime , " against which no scrutiny of one 's own side is felt to be necessary , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the party of " freedom , faith , and human dignity . " Once a conflict has been sorted this way , the ordinary journalistic and theological discipline of checking one 's own assumptions against one 's own tradition 's record simply stops being applied , and stops being felt as necessary . That is the tribalist deceit named at the outset of this response , and it is visible not in any single sentence of the article but in its overall architecture . <p> The Aura of Light : A Selective Reading of Mystical Testimony <p> The article 's opening " fact " is Mahmoud Ahmadinejad 's account of a mystical sensation during a 2005 address to the United Nations . It is presented as a uniquely alarming data point , " a rare glimpse into the spiritual beliefs that animate Iran 's most powerful leaders . " Set aside , for a moment , whether a single subjective report from one former president , out of office since 2013 , can bear the interpretive weight the article assigns it . Consider instead the article 's implicit claim that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> It is not . It is on record , from the public transcript of a 2019 interview conducted in Jerusalem , that the sitting United States Secretary of State was asked whether President Trump had been " raised by God " to protect the Jewish people from Iran , and responded by comparing the situation to the Book of Esther , in which Iran is cast typologically as Haman , the official who plotted a genocide ( Pompeo ) . That is not a private citizen 's mystical anecdote recalled years afterward . It is the chief diplomat of the most powerful state on earth , in office , affirming on the record that current American policy toward Iran maps onto a biblical genocide narrative . If Ahmadinejad 's aura is admissible evidence of dangerous theology animating a state 's nuclear posture , Pompeo 's Esther framing is at minimum equally admissible evidence of dangerous theology animating a nuclear superpower 's foreign policy toward that same state . The article cites the first and is silent about the second . That silence is not an oversight ; it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ appears in the " Cyrus paradigm " documented by Boyer , whereby a demonstrably secular president was cast by influential religious constituencies as a divinely appointed instrument comparable to the Persian king who authorised the return of the Jewish exiles , in order to justify treating his embassy relocation and Golan Heights recognition as " divine milestones " rather than ordinary diplomatic acts ( Boyer , p.312 ) . A mystical framework was applied , publicly , by influential American religious and political figures , to explain and celebrate concrete shifts in the foreign policy of the state that maintains the world 's largest nuclear arsenal and the most extensive network of overseas military bases in history . This is a " faith fact " fully as newsworthy as anything Ahmadinejad said at the podium in 2005 , and it is considerably more consequential , because it was not a rhetorical aside but an operative justification cited by an administration that actually altered the diplomatic map of the Middle East . <p> The article states that " Iranian leaders follow a radical interpretation of Islamic prophecy , " as though @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ whole . The comparative study , drawing on serious scholarship of Twelver Shi'ism , tells a more complicated story . Classical Twelver doctrine is overwhelmingly quietist : a millennium-long tradition of intizar , patient waiting , grounded in the judgement that no human government during the Imam 's occultation can claim his full authority , and that attempting to force the timetable of redemption is a form of presumption ( Sachedina , p.67 ) . Khomeini 's doctrine of wilayat al-faqih , which does grant a jurist expansive political authority , remains contested within the tradition itself , including by senior clerics in the Najaf tradition , who continue to reject it as a departure from settled doctrine ( Momen ) . Even within the constitutional and clerical establishment the study describes , the more explicitly accelerationist statements on record -- Hojatoleslam Ali Saeedi 's remark that the Revolutionary Guard functions to " pave the way " for the Mahdi , or Mehdi Taeb 's call to " remove the obstacles " to his return -- come from mid-ranking clerical figures addressing an institutional audience , not from the sitting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pronouncement ( qtd. in " Mahdism " ) . <p> None of this excuses or minimises what is genuinely troubling in the constitutional language the study quotes directly : the 1979 Constitution 's assignment of an " ideological mission of jihad " to Iran 's armed forces is a matter of public record , not inference , and deserves the scrutiny the article wants to give it ( Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran ) . But an argument that moves from " this constitutional clause exists " and " these clerics said this in 2012 and 2015 " to " Iranian leaders " as an undifferentiated category has skipped the entire question of how contested , marginal , and internally opposed the accelerationist reading actually is . The article performs exactly the manoeuvre the comparative study warns against throughout : it treats a minority hermeneutic as though it were the settled position of two hundred million people , and of the state that governs eighty million of them . <p> It is also worth noting what the article omits about the historical construction of the doctrine it treats @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Mahdi does not appear in the Qur'an at all , and that the doctrine of occultation itself took roughly two centuries to be rationalised into settled teaching by scholars such as al-Kulayni , Ibn Babawayh , and al-Shaykh al-Mufid , working through what one specialist calls a genuine communal " identity crisis , " following disputed reports about whether the eleventh Imam had even left an heir ( Amir-Moezzi ) . A doctrine assembled this gradually , out of contested and sometimes contradictory material , is not the kind of fixed , univocal programme the article implies when it speaks of Iranian leaders as though they were simply reading instructions from a single unambiguous page . Twelver jurisprudence developed its own internal science of chain-of-transmission criticism , isnad , specifically to prevent weakly attested reports about " signs " and the Sufyani from being elevated to the status of settled doctrine ( Momen ) . The extremist reading the article treats as definitive is one that has had to override this internal discipline , not one that flows naturally from it . An article willing to explain that distinction @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It chose not to . <p> The Missing Mirror -- Christian Zionism 's Own Accelerationist Theology <p> If the test for " dangerous theology " is a doctrine that treats catastrophic conflict as a desirable precursor to cosmic renewal , then dispensationalist Christian Zionism passes that test on its own terms , by its own proponents ' own description . The prophetic sequence the study summarises from Daniel , Ezekiel , and Revelation , as read by this movement , requires , among its stages , a seven-year Tribulation of global suffering and a climactic invasion of Israel -- Armageddon -- before Christ 's return ( Weber , p.214 ) . Because this sequence is read as a fixed timetable rather than a symbolic assurance , any political development that appears to advance a stage of it is treated , within the movement 's extreme wing , as independently desirable regardless of human cost . This is not a caricature drawn by hostile outsiders . It is the plain content of a system whose own founding literature is available in print , whose popular expositors -- Hal Lindsey 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- have sold in the tens of millions of copies across the American religious market , and whose organised political arm , Christians United for Israel , describes itself as the largest pro-Israel organisation in the United States , claiming a membership in the tens of millions ( " Christians United for Israel " ) . <p> The study goes further , identifying the specific ethical consequence that the article 's own framework should , by its own logic , treat as alarming : a theology of fatalism regarding nuclear war . " If the world is destined to be consumed by fire before being remade by God , there is little theological incentive for nuclear disarmament , environmental stewardship , or long-term international cooperation , " and war becomes " the clearing of the stage for the Kingdom of Heaven " rather than a failure of statecraft to be avoided ( Halsell , p.21 ) . This is , structurally and precisely , the same " theological MAD " that the article implicitly accuses Tehran of harbouring : annihilation is not feared but anticipated . The difference is that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A reader relying solely on " The Dangerous Theology Behind Iran 's Nuclear Ambitions " would never learn that an American religious-political movement with tens of millions of adherents holds a parallel doctrine , has organised a national lobbying apparatus around it , and has demonstrably shaped the foreign policy of a nuclear superpower through it -- documented not through hostile speculation but through the organisation 's own published statements of purpose and its own account of its legislative victories ( Durbin ; " Christians United for Israel ( CUFI ) " ) . <p> The Missing Mirror -- Messianic Jewish Zionism and the Temple Mount <p> A second silence in the article concerns radical religious Zionism within Israel itself . The study traces a direct theological line from Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook 's reinterpretation of secular Zionism as an unwitting instrument of divine redemption , through his son Zvi Yehuda Kook 's post-1967 doctrine that the conquest of the West Bank and East Jerusalem was " the beginning of the Messianic Age , " to the 1974 founding of Gush Emunim , whose own historiography records that its members @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Gush Emunim " ; Inbari ) . This is not a fringe historical curiosity . It is the acknowledged ideological ancestor of the settlement movement that governs the legal and demographic status of millions of people in the occupied territories today . <p> More directly relevant to the article 's own framework -- which treats the desire to " hasten " a divine timetable through manufactured chaos as the defining mark of dangerous theology -- is the documented history of the Jewish Underground . Between 1979 and 1984 , a clandestine group composed principally of Gush Emunim settlers developed an operational plan , using stolen military ordnance and detailed structural reconnaissance , to destroy the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque on the Temple Mount , reasoning that their removal would trigger a war so catastrophic that God would be compelled to intervene ( " Jewish Underground " ) . This is not a rhetorical claim inferred from a speech . It is a matter of Israeli court record : twenty-seven defendants were tried , fifteen convicted in 1985 , and the group 's own second-in-command testified that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ abomination , " and told the court that history would vindicate the plot ( " Jewish Underground Members Found Guilty " ) . No comparable court record of an operationalised , materiel-supported plot to trigger the apocalypse appears anywhere in the article 's account of Iran . If concrete , prosecuted , sentenced conspiracy is the standard of dangerousness , extreme religious Zionism clears a bar that the article 's chosen evidence -- a subjective mystical anecdote and a handful of speeches -- does not . <p> The institutional afterlife of this theology is , if anything , more disquieting than the plot itself , because it has moved from the criminal fringe into state-adjacent respectability . The Temple Institute , founded in 1987 , publishes without euphemism a mission " to do all in our limited power to bring about the building of the Holy Temple in our time " on the site currently occupied by the Islamic sanctuary , receives public funding from Israeli government ministries , and conducts tours of the Temple Mount under state police protection , even though the Israeli government does not officially endorse @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ; Berkowitz et al . ) . A movement whose stated object is the eventual removal of a rival faith 's holiest structures , operating with state funding and state police protection , is a considerably more institutionally embedded phenomenon than a hadith-quoting cleric addressing an audience of Revolutionary Guards . The article 's silence on this point is not a matter of space . It is a matter of which " specks " the author was willing to see . <p> Nor is the underlying logic confined to the Temple Mount specifically . The same hermeneutic that treats the physical conquest of land as a non-negotiable religious commandment , superseding ordinary political ethics and international law , has produced a typological reading in which the biblical enemy Amalek -- whose memory scripture commands to be blotted out -- is applied by extremist theologians to contemporary Palestinian populations , converting a territorial and political dispute into a cosmic struggle in which compromise itself becomes theological betrayal . Yehuda Etzion , identified in the court proceedings as the Jewish Underground 's second-in-command , described the Islamic structures on the Mount as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reproduced in the historical record , framed the plot 's intended success in explicitly redemptive terms , as the event that would open " another chapter " in Israel 's history ( qtd. in " Yehuda Etzion " ) . This is precisely the pattern the article insists is uniquely Iranian : a named , identifiable religious-political actor treating the deliberate manufacture of catastrophic conflict as a sacred labour rather than a crime to be prevented . The difference is that in this case the actor was tried , sentenced , and remains on the public court record -- which ought to make the case easier for a careful writer to cite , not harder . <p> Constitutions , Institutions , and the Question of Scale <p> The article treats the Iranian constitutional text assigning the armed forces an " ideological mission of jihad " as uniquely damning ( Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran ) . It is a fair point of concern , documented in ratified law rather than rumour . But institutional embedding of accelerationist theology is not confined to Tehran 's statute book . Christians @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advocacy through organised congressional summit visits and mass communication campaigns , credited by the organisation itself with helping to secure continued Iron Dome funding , legislation restricting aid conditioned on Palestinian Authority payments , the 2018 embassy relocation , the 2019 Golan Heights recognition , and emergency military assistance legislation following October 2023 ( " Christians United for Israel ( CUFI ) " ) . This is an advocacy pipeline running directly into the legislature and executive branch of the country that supplies , arms , and diplomatically shields the other party to the conflict the article is nominally worried about . <p> The comparison the article invites , once its own standard is applied evenly , is therefore not " Iran 's radical theology " versus " American Christian hope . " It is one constitutionally embedded ideological mandate inside a regionally significant but heavily sanctioned military , set against a state-funded Temple restoration project operating under police protection inside a nuclear-armed state , set against tens of millions strong lobbying organisations with a documented record of moving the foreign policy of the world 's dominant military power . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ second and third cases are not obviously the lesser danger . They may reasonably be judged the greater one , for the reason developed in the next section . <p> The Military Asymmetry -- Why Scale Changes the Moral Calculus <p> This is the crux of the present response . A theology of hastened apocalypse is dangerous in direct proportion to the destructive capacity available to the people who hold it . A minor cleric who believes chaos will summon the Mahdi is a matter of concern . A minor cleric who believes chaos will summon the Mahdi and who commands ten thousand aircraft , a nuclear arsenal exceeding five thousand warheads , and permanent basing on every continent is a matter of civilisational emergency . Global military power in the present century is not evenly distributed ; it is concentrated , overwhelmingly , in the United States and its closest allies . The United States alone accounts for a larger share of global military expenditure than the next ten states combined , maintains the only truly global network of overseas bases , and holds , together with its NATO @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ warheads . Israel , though it does not officially confirm the fact , is widely assessed to be the sole nuclear-armed state in the Middle East , and it is the recipient of the largest sustained programme of American military assistance given to any country in the world . <p> Iran , by contrast , possesses no nuclear weapons , operates an air force built substantially on airframes decades old , and has spent much of the past two decades under some of the most extensive sanctions regimes ever assembled , specifically constraining its military modernisation . This is not offered as a claim that Iran 's conduct is therefore benign , nor that its proxy network across Lebanon , Syria , Iraq , Yemen , and Gaza is anything other than a serious regional problem , as the article correctly notes . It is offered to make a narrower and , this response argues , decisive point : when the article asks American Christians to worry about the fusion of apocalyptic theology with military capacity , the fusion that should worry them most , on grounds of sheer destructive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ largest stockpile of destructive capacity on the planet -- which is to say , within the American and allied Israeli military-political complex , not within the comparatively constrained Iranian one . A spark is more dangerous in a room full of dynamite than in a room with a single match . The article spends its entire length examining the match and never once glances at the dynamite . <p> This is also why the article 's implicit prescription -- " supporting a strong American defence posture " and treating diplomacy as inherently insufficient -- should trouble a reader more , not less , once the theological analysis is applied symmetrically . If accelerationist eschatology genuinely degrades a state 's capacity for rational deterrence calculation , as the article argues in Iran 's case , then the demonstrated presence of a structurally identical eschatology inside the policymaking culture of the state holding the overwhelming preponderance of the world 's military power is the more urgent finding , not a footnote to be omitted . <p> The Co-Dependent Triangle the Article Refuses to See <p> The comparative study describes what it terms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ eschatologies examined treats the radicalism of the other two as confirmation of its own prophetic timeline , so that provocation on one side supplies theological oxygen to the others . A ritual provocation at the Temple Mount by Jewish extremists is read by Shia radicals as proof of the " Roman " assault on Islam 's third holiest site , justifying proxy mobilisation ; that mobilisation is in turn read by Christian Zionists as the " rumours of war " that confirm the approaching Rapture ; and the resulting Western alarm licenses further settlement activity , further arms transfers , and further apocalyptic rhetoric on the Israeli and American side . This is not a chain with one villain and two victims . It is a closed loop that all three radicalisms need in order to keep confirming themselves . <p> The article breaks into this loop at exactly one point -- Tehran -- and describes only the momentum arriving from that single direction , as though the loop had no other segments . This is not merely an incomplete picture ; it actively obscures the mechanism by which Iranian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ phenomenon , amplified by the very Temple Mount provocations and embassy-relocation triumphalism that Western radical theology has helped to produce . An article genuinely concerned with defusing apocalyptic danger in the region would have to examine the whole loop . An article that examines only one segment of it , while asking its readers to fund and arm the other two segments without reservation , is not analysing danger . It is administering it . <p> Deterrence , MAD , and the Selective Application of " Danger " <p> The article 's most serious claim is that Iran 's Mahdist worldview may render " traditional diplomatic incentives and deterrents " insufficient , because leaders who believe they are divinely appointed to hasten a messianic age may not respond to ordinary rational calculation . This is a claim worth taking seriously , and the comparative study takes it seriously , describing the concept of tamhis -- purgation through trial -- as a hermeneutic capable of reframing catastrophic conflict , even nuclear conflict , as necessary divine sifting rather than tragedy ( Sachedina , p.145 ) . <p> But the same study @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ side of the ledger , under the heading of " theological MAD " : a doctrine in which " annihilation is not feared but anticipated , " because catastrophic global war is read as the necessary precursor to eternal renewal ( Halsell , p.45 ) . If this reasoning genuinely disables rational deterrence when found in a Shia cleric 's reading of the Sufyani traditions , it must , by the same logic , disable rational deterrence when found in an American pastor 's reading of Ezekiel 38 or an Israeli seminarian 's reading of the Kookist doctrine of active redemption . The article can not have it both ways : it can not claim that apocalyptic theology corrodes rational strategic calculation only when the theology in question belongs to its geopolitical rival , and remains harmless background colour when it belongs to its geopolitical patron . Deterrence theory does not check the passport of the believer before deciding whether his eschatology has compromised his judgement . <p> The mechanism by which this corrosion of deterrence proceeds is , moreover , identical across all three cases examined , which is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ argument would need to grapple with all three rather than one . In each tradition , a political rival is first relocated from the category of a negotiating counterpart into the category of a typological enemy -- the " Great Satan , " the " King of the North , " " Amalek " -- and once that relocation has occurred , the ordinary ethical restraints that govern conflict between neighbours , including proportionality and the protection of civilians , are treated as secular weaknesses rather than binding obligations . It is this typological othering , not the mere existence of apocalyptic belief , that does the actual work of disabling deterrence , because a typological enemy can not , by definition , be negotiated with ; negotiating with Amalek or with the Great Satan is not diplomacy but capitulation . An article that wants its readers to fear this mechanism in Tehran , while asking them , in the same breath , to adopt an uncomplicated us-versus-them posture toward Iran -- " the values of freedom , faith , and human dignity that Americans hold dear " set against @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- is not warning its readers away from the mechanism . It is inviting them to practise a milder version of it . <p> Prayer as Policy -- The Article 's Own Theological Prescription <p> It is worth pausing on the article 's own constructive proposal , because it illustrates the same asymmetry in miniature . Having diagnosed Iran 's problem as the fusion of theology with statecraft , the article 's remedy is explicitly theological : " Prayer remains our most powerful weapon . We must pray for the protection of Israel , for wisdom for American leaders ... and even for the Iranian people themselves , who suffer under a repressive theocratic regime that has squandered their nation 's potential in pursuit of a false messiah . " Whatever the pastoral value of this prayer , it is worth noticing what it does rhetorically : it reserves rational agency -- " wisdom " -- for American leaders , reserves victimhood for the Iranian people , and reserves the accusation of false messianism exclusively for the other side 's theology , while asking readers to view their own side @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A call to " pray for the protection of Israel , " issued in the same breath as a call to support " a strong American defence posture , " is not a retreat from the fusion of theology and geopolitics the article claims to be worried about . It is a restatement of that fusion from the other seat at the table . <p> Removing the Log First <p> None of the foregoing is an argument that Iran 's Mahdist accelerationists do not exist , that the constitutional language the article cites is not real , or that the region 's dangers are imaginary . They are real , documented , and worth the concern the article expresses . The argument is narrower and , this response submits , more important : an essay that isolates one civilisation 's theological extremists , generalises them into " Iran 's leadership " as a whole , and sets them against an unexamined , idealised portrait of its own tradition has not identified the danger of religious eschatology . It has performed the danger of religious eschatology , in miniature , by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ world into the illuminated and the deluded , the rational and the fanatical , without applying a single evidentiary standard to both halves of the division . <p> Once that standard is applied evenly , the picture the article paints does not survive . Constitutionally embedded accelerationist doctrine exists on more than one side of this conflict . Court-documented conspiracies to trigger apocalyptic war through the destruction of a rival faith 's holy site exist on more than one side . Heads of state and cabinet-level officials publicly framing geopolitical rivalry in explicitly messianic and genocide-narrative terms exist on more than one side . And crucially , the side possessing the greater capacity to turn any of this theology into an irreversible catastrophe is not the sanctioned regional power with no nuclear weapons and a fraction of the world 's military spending . It is the alliance that commands the largest military machine ever assembled , entangled with the region 's only nuclear arsenal . If the log is anywhere close to the size the comparative study 's own analysis suggests , it is not in Tehran that Western readers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is in the mirror . <p> A Note on the Contested Ground <p> Fairness requires acknowledging that this argument , like the article it answers , is contestable , and that reasonable people read the same record differently . Several counterpoints deserve to be stated rather than buried . <p> First , aggregate military power is not the same thing as propensity to act on apocalyptic theology in a given instance . A critic could reasonably argue that comparing the size of the American and Israeli arsenals to Iran 's is a category error , if the actual question is which government 's stated intentions and recent conduct pose the more proximate risk of triggering deliberate catastrophe , and Iran 's own officials have , on the public record , issued explicit and repeated threats against Israel 's existence that have no precise Israeli or American analogue . <p> Second , the political structures differ in kind and not only in degree : The United States and Israel are contested electoral democracies , in which theological lobbying groups compete , and sometimes lose , against secular constituencies , courts , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ al-faqih structure places ultimate authority with an unelected cleric largely insulated from electoral correction . A critic could argue that this institutional difference matters more than the comparative headcounts of accelerationist believers on each side . <p> Third , the comparative study on which this response leans explicitly declines to rank the three eschatologies against one another , and warns against exactly the kind of comparative " danger ranking " this response constructs from its material . A careful reader should treat that warning as a genuine limitation on the argument above , not merely a disclaimer to be brushed past . <p> Finally , the empirical question of Iran 's actual nuclear intentions and timeline , and the empirical question of how much causal weight Mahdist theology carries in Tehran 's decision-making relative to ordinary considerations of regime survival and deterrence , remain genuinely disputed among specialists , and neither the original article nor this response should be read as having settled them . <p> Bibliography <p> Amir-Moezzi , Mohammad Ali . We explain . <p> Why is Israel building these structures ? <p> These giant earthen walls and raised berms ( barriers ) are fundamentally altering the physical geography of Gaza , effectively solidifying the 45-km Yellow Line that separates Israeli military-controlled territory in the east from Palestinian-controlled areas in the west . These barriers may also fit in with Israel 's goal of dividing the territory into isolated northern and southern enclaves to allow forces to regulate civilian movement . <p> Ultimately , such a barrier that divides Gaza will hurt the prospects of a contiguous territory , and , in turn , statehood . <p> An old practice <p> Earthen berms and ramparts are among the oldest architectural defensive structures in human history , dating back to ancient siege warfare and Roman circumvallation lines . Historically , field armies threw up massive earthworks to enclose besieged cities or protect garrison boundaries at low engineering costs . <p> Modern warfare experts and military engineers see earth berms as structures that offer distinct advantages : They are easy and quick to be built ; they provide better defence against heavy artillery and rocket fire and provide height to the defensive posts and surveillance sensors . <p> As far as the Israeli-Palestinian conflict is concerned , the barriers have evolved across several decades . It all began with the Gaza perimeter fence that was built in 1994 following the Oslo Accords to encircle @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The Israeli West-Bank barrier near Ramallah . Wikimedia Commons <p> Since 2002 , Israel has been building a planned 700-km barrier to separate the West Bank from Jerusalem and Israel . This barrier is a multi-layered structure combining concrete walls , fences , radar and patrol roads designed to separate Israeli towns from West Bank urban centers . <p> Then came the subterranean anti-tunnel barriers along the Gaza perimeter . These are underground concrete walls and electronic sensor arrays aimed at detecting subterranean excavation . <p> Where else have earth berms been used ? <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Setting up earthen berms is a solution that has been serving as a low-cost yet effective means of enforcing territorial separation and asymmetric control in major geopolitical conflicts globally . <p> The Moroccan Wall ( " The Berm " ) in Western Sahara -- a massive 2,700-km sand and stone embankment fortified with landmines and artillery -- was built by Morocco in the 1980s to separate its controlled territory from the Polisario Front . Several more walls were built over the years . <p> Location of the Moroccan sand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Israeli military itself deployed this engineering concept along the Suez Canal from 1968 to 1973 ; the Bar Lev Line featured a formidable 20-to-25-metre-high sand rampart designed to block Egyptian amphibious counterattacks . <p> Similar applications of elevated earth mounding paired with sensor technology can also be found slicing across the Korean Demilitarized Zone ( DMZ ) and along stretches of the Syrian -- Turkish border . All these examples illustrate how modern armed forces rely on such earthworks to freeze front lines , manage border security and enforce long-term spatial divisions . <p> Impact on any future Palestinian State <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Geographer Merav Amir , in her 2017 research paper Revisiting Politicide : State Annihilation in Israel/Palestine , notes that the severe restrictions on Gaza ( which began right after the 2005 Disengaement ) that was gradually turned into fully-fledged blockade , has left it completely isolated from the rest of the world . This has also posed severe structural challenges to the establishment of a viable , contiguous Palestinian state . It will also affect domestic supply chains . <p> Most importantly , the blockades will prevent a large number of displaced Palestinians from returning to their homes and neighborhoods destroyed by Israeli bombing in the ongoing war . @@139260488 <h> Five years of exceptional measures in Tunisia : Systematic erosion of human rights and rule of law <p> Geneva -- Five years following the implementation of exceptional measures in Tunisia , there has been a significant and structural decline in the rule of law and human rights protections . The measures announced by President Kais Saied on 25 July 2021 have evolved from temporary measures into a lasting authoritarian regime . This system is built on centralising control over state institutions and transforming the judiciary into a tool for retribution and political exclusion . <p> This system has deployed an arsenal of arbitrary laws to suppress the opposition and stifle civic space and freedom of expression through campaigns of arrests and prolonged pretrial detention , alongside the institutionalisation of incitement rhetoric that has led to grave and systematic violations affecting citizens , migrants , and asylum seekers alike . This clearly contradicts Tunisia 's international legal obligations and transforms state institutions from protectors into tools that suppress basic rights and undermine the progress of the democratic transition . <p> In a key move to consolidate one-man rule , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ judiciary as a political instrument to eliminate opposition . This course started with the dissolution of the legitimate Supreme Judicial Council in February 2022 , which was replaced by a provisional council under complete control of the executive authorities . It resulted in the arbitrary dismissal of 57 judges by presidential decree , with the executive authorities continuing to systematically refuse to comply with the Administrative Court 's rulings that ordered a stay on most of these dismissals . <p> This blatant interference in the course of justice has been accompanied by an unprecedented militarisation of the judiciary , with the referral of dozens of civilians , including politicians , journalists , and lawyers , to military courts to be tried for political opinions or stances , in flagrant violation of individuals ' right to a fair trial before a competent and independent civilian court and in explicit contradiction with Tunisia 's obligations under Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights . <p> The domination of the judiciary has been accompanied by the creation of an arsenal of arbitrary legislation , foremost among it Decree 54 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ most enduring instrument for stifling free speech in the country . Article 24 of the Decree appears to be drafted in broadly worded and undisciplined terms to intimidate opponents under the pretext of " combating false news . " <p> Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor observed repeated and systematic reports of dozens of journalists , lawyers , and bloggers being investigated and harshly sentenced simply for publishing posts or making critical media statements . This pattern has led to widespread self-censorship , weakened public discourse , and transformed government criticism into a criminal offence that warrants security and judicial action . As a result , the core of the right to freedom of expression has been undermined , fostering a culture of impunity within the executive apparatus . <p> The deployment of this legal and judicial arsenal has led to a dangerous escalation in arbitrary arrests and the criminalisation of freedom of opinion and political work . Tunisia 's prison population has risen to more than 33,000 in 2025 , compared with about 23,000 in 2022 , with overcrowding rates exceeding 200 per cent in some detention centres , according to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> This record rise reflects a government policy of systematically exaggerating the use of prolonged pretrial detention and exceeding legal custody limits , aiming to establish it as a hidden form of punishment imposed beforehand and outside the scope of justice . <p> The targeting of the opposition culminated in late 2025 with unfair mass trials that lacked the most basic guarantees of a fair trial , in which severe prison sentences ranging from 5 to 45 years were handed down to several activists and politicians in the case known as " Conspiracy Against State Security " . This case was followed by the immediate arrest of prominent leaders , who were then sentenced to lengthy terms . These sentences were based on vague charges and lacked any tangible material evidence , relying exclusively on the criminalisation of peaceful political meetings and activities , in a manner that explicitly breaches the procedural guarantees protecting individuals from arbitrary detention set out in the relevant international instruments . <p> Over the past five years , the targeted suppression of media has significantly increased , facilitated by security and judicial enforcement of Decree @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from the National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists have recorded over 1,000 attacks on journalists and media outlets since the implementation of these exceptional measures . These include criminal prosecutions of multiple journalists and the imprisonment of several , often for publishing content that criticises the authorities . <p> This systematic pattern of prosecutions reflects an official orientation towards criminalising journalism and undermining the right to freedom of expression , constituting a flagrant violation of the guarantees enshrined in the Tunisian Constitution itself , in particular its Article 37 , which guarantees media freedom and prohibits prior censorship , as well as undermining international obligations under Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights . It establishes a coercive environment that lacks the most basic legal protection for media workers , in a manner that disables their oversight role and strikes at the core of civil and political liberties in the country . <p> The erosion of the democratic path has taken an institutional form through the annulment of the 2014 constitution and its replacement with the 2022 constitution , which was drafted unilaterally . This constitution abolished @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , concentrated executive and legislative powers in the hands of the President , marginalised the role of parliament , and reduced it to a formal cover stripped of any real oversight powers . This change undermined the principle of separation of powers and created an overly presidential system that endorses concentrated authority , depriving the Tunisian people of their right to participate freely in politics and manage public affairs . <p> The monopolisation of state institutions has extended to independent bodies that are the most prominent guarantors of the democratic transition , in particular the Independent High Authority for Elections , whose independence was entirely undermined by presidential decisions amending its composition and by the direct appointment of its members by the President . This policy has stripped subsequent electoral contests of any standards of transparency and integrity , turning them into mere procedural waypoints for perpetuating the existing authority amid record popular and political boycotts . This represents a clear breach of Tunisia 's obligations under Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights , which guarantees citizens the right to take part in genuine periodic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ political contests has led to the systematic exclusion of key competitors through their imprisonment , prosecution , or disqualification via exclusionary laws . These authoritarian tactics have transformed Tunisian politics from a pluralistic space into a closed arena entirely subject to the executive 's engineering , thereby disabling Tunisians ' right to free choice and undermining the very legitimacy of the institutions emerging from this unilateral course , confirming that the exceptional measures were nothing but a cover for dismantling Tunisia 's nascent democracy and a return to authoritarian rule . <p> The dismantling of the institutional structure has been accompanied by a deliberate strategy to poison the public discourse and criminalise civic efforts . This has been carried out through official rhetoric that promotes exclusion , with high-level leaders consistently using specific language to label opponents and independent activists as traitors , collaborators , or conspirators . Such discourse creates a hostile political and social climate , framing critical voices as threats to national security . This approach undermines social cohesion and turns state institutions into tools for enforcing a singular narrative , thereby erasing diversity and criminalising legitimate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , now serving as political cover and a mandate for security forces to intensify repressive measures against civic and political figures without fear of accountability . It fosters impunity , encouraging pro-government groups to intimidate and publicly slander opponents , effectively institutionalising violence . This undermines international obligations that call on authorities to safeguard individuals from incitement to hatred and violence , rather than being its origin . <p> Official incitement campaigns are directly causing strict restrictions on civil society organisations and independent rights groups . These groups face ongoing targeting through threats of amending the Decree governing their work , aiming to cut their funding and control their activities . This reflects a clear intention to eliminate independent oversight bodies that monitor abuses and defend human rights in the country . <p> The scope of serious violations caused by this authoritarian approach has expanded from targeting citizens to also harming vulnerable migrants and asylum seekers from sub-Saharan Africa . President Kais Saied 's televised speech on 21 February 2023 incited unprecedented hatred and racist sentiments against these groups . This created an institutional climate that led security forces to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in a severe humanitarian and human rights crisis that starkly opposes Tunisia 's human rights obligations . <p> The security approach adopted by the authorities has resulted in the documentation of appalling violations , including mass expulsions , arbitrary detention , and the abandonment of hundreds of migrants , including women , children , and registered asylum seekers , in remote desert areas along the borders with Libya and Algeria , where they were left in harsh climatic conditions , unable to access food , water , and shelter . This has led to documented humanitarian tragedies and numerous deaths , dehumanising them and endangering their lives , far from any oversight or urgent relief intervention . <p> The mass expulsions and forced returns of migrants and asylum seekers clearly violate international human rights and refugee laws . This includes breaching the principle of non-refoulement , a binding rule of customary law , and directly contravenes the 1951 Refugee Convention and the African Charter on Human and Peoples ' Rights . <p> The situation in Tunisia is more than just a series of violations ; it represents a deliberate and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The state of exception has been used as an authoritarian tool to weaken institutional protections for human rights . This process involves manipulating the law to favour those in power , removing legal protections for individuals and civil society , and transforming publicly guaranteed freedoms into privileges that the executive can unilaterally assign or revoke . <p> The breakdown of Tunisia 's justice system and the intentional abolition of domestic redress directly violate its international human rights treaty commitments . Allowing impunity and protecting security and executive authorities from independent judicial oversight creates a fundamental breach of the principles of the civil state . This situation imposes a legal and moral duty on the United Nations and the international community to move beyond mere diplomacy and condemnation . They must implement practical accountability measures to prevent this authoritarian regression from becoming permanent and to address the systemic collapse of rights and freedoms in Tunisia . <p> Tunisian authorities must immediately end all exceptional measures that established this authoritarian course and eroded the rule of law ; urgently and unconditionally release all political detainees , prisoners of conscience , journalists , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , foremost among them Decree 54 of 2022 ; cease referring civilians to military courts ; and restore the independence of the judiciary by reinstating the dismissed judges in accordance with the Administrative Court 's ruling . Euro-Med Monitor stresses that Tunisia must comply with its international obligations , provide legal and humanitarian protection to migrants and asylum seekers , and halt all practices of expulsion and forcible removal . <p> The United Nations and its relevant bodies , such as the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights , the Special Procedures , and the Special Rapporteurs on the independence of judges and lawyers , on freedom of opinion and expression , and on the human rights of migrants , should urgently and closely follow the scale of the human rights deterioration taking place in Tunisia . It is essential to tighten field oversight , produce regular reports on these ongoing violations , and activate international accountability measures to ensure that those responsible for dismantling state institutions and violating individuals ' rights are held accountable . @@139309236 <h> Climate overheating is a story , and human survival depends on how we tell that story . <p> Climate overheating is a story , and human survival depends on how we tell that story . It is a story about the ruling class , about the exploited , working masses , about organization and revolution . It is a story about capitalism , about unspeakable suffering , about politics , media , wealth and power . It is a story that Marxists will understand about a speculative end -- a matter of something destined to unfold , yet still beyond our capacity to imagine . It encompasses familiar themes of both a biblical apocalypse and the grand designs of history . I am only one story teller -- a struggling , uncertain , inadequate one , perhaps -- but the plot lies in front of me ( as it does for anyone to scrutinize ) with all of its compelling and epic subplots . <p> Climate overheating is not a fragmented narrative about local floods and wildfires . It exempts no one and meaningfully returns to global themes and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate into a riddle about carbon capture , sea walls and renewable energy , even if technical means of mitigation have to be deployed . We can easily miss the forest for the trees . Climate is a tale about the means of production , profit , and the divided working class . The ending , unlike in classical Marxism , may be one of brutal failure and utter collapse . But the final act will revolve around the working class as we react with outrage or surrender . <p> Climate overheating is a story about criminals and victims , about failure and salvation , about beguiling mirages , about futile half measures , habitual compromises and the rageful insistence of nature . <p> We live in the age of excess -- excess wealth , addiction , excess stuff straining walls , storage facilities , supply closets , attics , basements and landfills . The AMOC -- an acronym for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation , the system of ocean streams that delivers equatorial warmth to the North Atlantic , has been slowing down as the ocean absorbs heat from our greenhouse gasses . A stagnant ocean will cause Europe to freeze . Huh ? How do warming waters deliver an ice age ? You ask . <p> " The AMOC is driven by the formation of deep water near Greenland : Cold , salty water sinks for the simple reason that cold water is more dense than warm water , and salty water is more dense than fresh . This sinking pulls surface waters toward northern Europe from the east coast of the Americas and further south , powering a massive global conveyor belt of water that extends all the way down to the southern tip of Africa . But as the north warms thanks to climate change , its waters become less dense and therefore less inclined to sink . The current slows . This pulls less salty water up from Africa , making the water in the north @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The current slows more . Melting ice from Greenland freshens the waters further , exacerbating the problem . Eventually , this feedback loop shuts the current down . <p> Something similar has happened before : An AMOC shutdown played havoc with the planet 12,000 years ago , when the end of the last ice age dumped huge amounts of fresh water into the northern ocean . This plunged Europe back into ice-age-like conditions , with Greenland , for example , cooling by a stunning 18 degrees F ( 10 degrees C ) . " The effects are amongst the most drastic we have seen in the paleorecord , " says ( climate scientist , Stefan ) Rahmstorf . " We really do n't want this to happen . " " <p> No matter how much " we really do n't want this to happen , " it will happen , perhaps sooner rather than later if global capitalism fails to summon mass resistance . Fast decarbonisation of energy systems is necessary . But we also need a major shift away from overconsumption towards " sufficiency " . This would involve a sharp reduction in labour hours and the use of raw materials , along with big changes in consumption patterns , food habits , land use and forest cover . Financing and politically sustaining decarbonisation and sufficiency will require a drastic reduction in inequality of income , wealth and power , between countries and within them . " The basic narrative must be the foundation for political organization , particularly among poor and working people . <p> Climate overheating is a global issue that can not be solved by nationalistic politics . Nationalists default to racist , anti-immigrant tropes , leading to war and genocidal solutions as a distraction from the true crimes of the past centuries -- the unfettered rule of fossil fuel capitalists , animal agriculture and giant tech corporations ( with its insatiable passion for fossil fuels ) . Underpopulated countries like Canada , the US and Russia will have to share their good fortune with poor people driven from their homelands by capitalist behaviors of extraction , pollution and emissions . Survival is not about neoliberal nostalgia for an American ideology that never existed outside of fantasy . Survival will involve mass understanding of the emergency engulfing us . @@139309239 <h> The War that Moved the Geography of Power : What the 2026 Gulf War revealed about the new grammar of global power <h> On 28 February 2026 , in twelve hours , American and Israeli air power struck Iran nearly nine hundred times and killed its Supreme Leader . In retaliation , Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz . What the world discovered in the weeks that followed was not simply one more regional war . It was a live demonstration that , in the twenty-first century , power is measured less by the territory a state holds than by the flows -- oil , capital , data , insurance , confidence -- that it can keep moving , or interrupt . <p> The Strait That Stopped the World <p> At 03:17 Greenwich Mean Time , a fully laden crude-oil tanker slows before entering the Strait of Hormuz . Its captain is not thinking about geopolitics . He is thinking about wind speed , navigation , insurance premiums . Thousands of kilometres away , traders in Singapore watch the same strait not through binoculars but through the movement of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ banks revise inflation forecasts . Before a single missile is fired , the battlefield has already extended across the whole of the global economy . <p> The scene is not a literary device ; it describes , almost literally , what occurred . Within weeks of the war 's outbreak , some twenty thousand seafarers found themselves trapped aboard hundreds of vessels in the Gulf1 , unable to move and unwilling to risk the crossing . The war did not begin with that paralysis . It began with a realization : that modern civilization had become , perhaps irreversibly , dependent on the uninterrupted circulation of energy , capital , information , and maritime trade . <p> The Strait of Hormuz , through which close to a fifth of the world 's traded oil passes2 , ceased to be a mere shipping lane and became a test of globalization 's resilience . When Iran closed it on the evening of 28 February , the Revolutionary Guard announced over VHF radio that no vessel would be permitted to pass . The disruption was local . Its consequences were immediate and global @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of global oil supply at 10.1 million barrels a day in March alone -- the largest disruption of the oil market on record3 . By April , cumulative losses since February had reached 12.8 million barrels a day , with Gulf-state output still 14.4 million barrels below its pre-war level . A coordinated release of four hundred million barrels by the IEA 's thirty-two member states cushioned the shock without resolving it . <p> The oil price told the same story in a different language . Brent crude , at $83.58 on 3 March , reached $101.59 nine days later and $104.76 by mid-month4 . But the most revealing figure was not the one in the headlines . By April , as futures drifted back toward $97 in hope of a settlement , the price actually paid for a physically delivered cargo -- " Dated Brent " -- held near $132 . That thirty-five-dollar gap between paper and barrel measured something market sentiment could not : real scarcity . It also identified who was paying -- Gulf producers and Iraq losing an estimated $1.1 billion a day in revenue for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from Dresden to Oran met the same war at the pump and in the price of bread . <p> The shock did not stay confined to the oil market . Gold , already higher on the year , surged nearly 2 percent within hours to above $5,380 an ounce -- its highest level in weeks -- while J.P . Morgan 's commodities desk projected a further five-to-ten-point risk premium6 . Marine insurers moved just as fast : war-risk premiums for a seven-day Gulf transit , ordinarily near a quarter of one percent of hull value , spiked to ten percent within a fortnight before easing to roughly one percent by late March -- for a hundred-million-dollar tanker , a bill rising from about $250,000 to as much as $10 million for a single voyage7 . Gold , oil , and insurance are three separate flows in the vocabulary of this analysis ; within hours of each other , they moved as a single system . <p> This economic cost should not obscure its human price . One seafarer , reached by reporters from Iraqi waters minutes after a nearby strike @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a Philippine-crewed vessel , a captain put the crossing to a vote among his twenty-seven men ; nearly all refused , choosing , in one sailor 's words , to go home alive9 . Off Bandar Abbas , a twenty-six-year-old Indian seafarer counted the weeks since he had last seen his family while watching drones set nearby ships ablaze -- one of some twenty-three thousand Indian nationals crewing the Gulf , three of whom were killed and one left missing10 . These are the voices the price charts never carry . <p> A War That No Longer Obeys Twentieth-Century Grammar <p> For more than a century , geopolitical thought rested on a single premise : that power follows geography . Mahan looked to the seas , Mackinder to the Eurasian heartland , Spykman to the rimland -- their disagreements were profound , but they shared one vocabulary : territory , frontier , strategic depth , lines of communication . <p> That vocabulary described the last century well . The Gulf War of 2026 obeys a different logic . Its object was not the permanent conquest of land , nor even @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ turned on maintaining -- or disrupting -- the circulation of systems on which distant societies depended : oil and gas , shipping and insurance , digital communications and financial settlement . The centre of gravity shifted . The battlefield no longer ended where the front line stopped ; it extended into ports , exchanges , data centres , energy markets . <p> " Power no longer resides solely in the possession of resources . It resides increasingly in the capacity to keep them moving under conditions of stress . " <p> This is the central proposition this dossier advances : the Gulf War of 2026 should be understood not as another regional conflict but as the first major war for the governance of global flows -- the first in which the capacity to sustain or sever the circulation of interconnected systems became the central strategic stake . This framework does not claim to replace classical geopolitics ; it integrates it with network theory , political economy , and the study of infrastructure . Susan Strange showed a generation ago that the deepest power is not the power that produces an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ outcomes are decided11 ; Farrell and Newman showed how interdependence , once celebrated as a guarantor of peace , could become an instrument of coercion12 . What 2026 made visible was the synthesis of both : power now consists of four distinct capacities -- to enable a strategic flow , to protect it , to redirect it when a route closes , or to deny it to a rival when coercion is the aim . <p> This framework has limits , and stating them matters , because a theory that explained everything would explain nothing . The contemporaneous war in Ukraine remains a contest for land in the oldest , strictest sense , fully intelligible without the vocabulary of flows -- and this analysis would be wrong to claim otherwise . Where dependence on complex circulation is absent , the older grammar of territory still governs . That boundary is precisely what makes the hypothesis testable rather than infinitely elastic : had the closure of Hormuz produced no strategic leverage , the thesis would have been refuted . Instead it reorganized , within weeks , the behaviour of governments , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Five Pillars for Measuring a Power That Has Changed Its Nature <p> From this analysis emerges a five-pillar architecture , summarized in a deliberately non-mathematical formula : strategic power is the product of connectivity , resilience , adaptability , legitimacy , and coordination . The choice of a multiplicative rather than additive form is not decorative -- it means a serious weakness in any one pillar can undermine the whole . A technologically advanced network without legitimacy remains politically brittle ; military superiority without coordination yields diminishing returns . <p> This framework inverts the very definition of victory . Where classical theory tied victory to conquest or the destruction of enemy forces , networked conflict imposes a complementary definition : victory now belongs to the actor able to preserve the functional continuity of its own essential systems while imposing disproportionate disruption on its adversary 's . Continuity becomes strategy ; resilience becomes deterrence . <p> Who Governs a War in Which Markets Decide as Much as Armies ? <p> For centuries , war was understood as the exclusive domain of sovereign states : governments declare it , armies fight it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ; it is no longer analytically sufficient . The Gulf War of 2026 unfolded within a far broader ecosystem of actors whose decisions shaped events without any one of them commanding a single soldier . <p> The U.S. Navy could secure a sea lane , and did -- escorting vessels through the strait , then imposing a blockade on Iranian ports after the Islamabad talks collapsed13 . But a warship can not compel an underwriter to lower a war-risk premium , nor force a commodity market to disregard uncertainty . When a fleet manager lost contact with a seized tanker , its stated priority was not the war effort but crew safety14 . Confidence itself had become an operational variable -- and confidence answers to no chain of command . <p> The insurance market demonstrated this better than any theory could . The Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization , Arsenio Dominguez , warned that the persistently high cost of maritime insurance was compounding shipowners ' strain even as conditions improved , and urged governments to press insurers to reprice risk against present conditions rather than the memory of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ private underwriters is , in miniature , the whole argument : the state that could destroy Iran 's bridges could not , by the same authority , instruct Lloyd 's of London . <p> Suez , Covid , Ukraine , the Red Sea , Taiwan : A Theory Under Test <p> No theory deserves trust unless it illuminates more than a single event . Five precedents , chosen for their diversity rather than their resemblance , put this one to the test . <p> The 1956 Suez Crisis offers the oldest and cleanest confirmation available : Britain and France won the military engagement and lost the war of legitimacy , forced into withdrawal by American financial pressure on the pound sterling -- the earliest proof that a canal can close by force while reopening , just as forcibly , on the diplomatic register16 . Covid-19 tests the framework 's edges rather than its centre : a global health shock paralyzed logistics , semiconductors , and cold chains without any actor seeking to exploit it deliberately , a reminder that systemic vulnerability exists independent of hostile intent . <p> Ukraine , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on closer inspection to be considerably more hybrid : alongside the front lines , a negotiated Black Sea grain corridor and financial sanctions routed through the SWIFT network made this a conflict in which territory and flows contested primacy simultaneously . The Red Sea campaign opened by Houthi attacks extends the Hormuz logic to a second theatre -- proof that a second-tier actor can tax global trade without ever deploying a navy . Taiwan , finally , occupies a different place , deliberately so : no crisis has yet tested its semiconductor ecosystem at the scale of a strait closure or open war . It appears here as a prospective case , not a confirmed one -- the theory ventures a wager it does not yet claim to have proven . <p> " What these cases share is not their resemblance , but the same lesson repeated in different forms : confidence breaks faster than it can be repaired . " <p> The Great Powers Tested by Flows <p> For centuries , the rise of great powers followed a familiar pattern : population , territory , resources , industrial and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ remain important ; they are no longer sufficient . The Gulf War put a different question to every major power : how effectively can it preserve the circulation of its critical systems under stress ? <p> The United States retains unrivalled military reach , a global alliance network , financial centrality -- but the very openness that is its strength is also the source of its exposure : five hundred troops wounded , eighteen killed since February , a Congress voting repeatedly to end a war it never authorized17 , months before a midterm election . China , by contrast , gained precisely by governing its own exposure : condemning the assassination of a head of state as a violation of the UN Charter while withholding any material military support18 . The European Union demonstrates a model resting less on centralized military power than on regulatory capacity -- but acutely exposed to energy shocks : Brussels warned that a war holding Brent near $100 could push euro-area inflation above 3 percent19 . <p> A Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas study , by economists Kilian , Plante , Richter , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ U.S. inflation by 5.2 points in March , before a partial reversal should the strait reopen ; a companion note from the Centre for Economic Policy Research put the more cautious full-year effect at 0.6 points on headline inflation20 . The convergence of two independent research teams , using different methods , on the same directional conclusion carries more weight than any single estimate . <p> A Theory That Exposes Itself to Criticism <p> The authority of any theoretical framework is measured as much by the objections it can survive as by the cases it explains . The heaviest comes from realism : in the tradition of Kenneth Waltz and John Mearsheimer , the structure of international politics remains anarchic and its currency remains material power ; institutions and networks are mere epiphenomena that evaporate the moment force is applied . The objection is serious , and partly right : no analysis ignoring military power could explain a war that opened with nine hundred air strikes . But American military supremacy destroyed Iran 's bridges and ports without securing surrender , and no fleet could restore the confidence on which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ circulation that passes through it . <p> Hal Brands and Michael Beckley , in a widely discussed essay , locate the gravest danger not in networks but in the closing demographic and material window of a rising China21 . Stephen Walt , for his part , faults America 's foreign-policy establishment for mistaking the management of global systems for a vital interest , when restraint would have served Washington better22 . These critiques , taken seriously here rather than dismissed , operate at a different level : they concern which wars a state should choose to fight ; this analysis concerns how the wars a state does choose to fight are actually conducted and resolved . <p> The hardest objection to dismiss remains circularity . If the war supplied both the material and the test of the theory , is the whole exercise anything more than an elaborate redescription of the same facts in the same vocabulary ? A single-case test can never fully dispel that suspicion -- which is precisely why the comparison with Suez , Covid , Ukraine , the Red Sea , and Taiwan matters : it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The final verdict belongs to time , not to this text . <p> The Map That Never Appears <p> Maps show borders . They colour states , mark capitals , trace mountains and rivers . But the map that actually governs the twenty-first century remains , for the most part , invisible . It is drawn in shipping lanes crossing oceans , in fibre-optic cables laid silently on the seabed , in energy corridors crossing deserts , in financial transactions moving through secured networks , in semiconductors travelling from a handful of factories to factories on every continent . <p> The Gulf War of 2026 illuminated this hidden map , and its deepest lesson may concern neither a single region nor a single conflict , but the nature of power itself . Civilizations endure not only because they conquer , but because they preserve the systems that allow societies to function . The future of international order may depend less on who dominates the world than on who can keep alive the flows that sustain it . <p> Empires once measured their power by the lands they ruled ; the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can protect , sustain , and restore . If that intuition holds , the Gulf War of 2026 will not be remembered as one regional conflict among others , but as the moment when the invisible geography of the modern world became impossible to ignore . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Laala Bechetoula is an independent Algerian historian , journalist and geopolitical analyst .
